passages.text: Heavy Metal Tolerance in Plants: Role of Transcriptomics, Proteomics, Metabolomics, and Ionomics

Heavy metal contamination of soil and water causing toxicity/stress has become one important constraint to crop productivity and quality. <sentence_start/>This situation has further worsened by the increasing population growth and inherent food demand. <sentence_start/>It has been reported in several studies that counterbalancing toxicity due to heavy metal requires complex mechanisms at molecular, biochemical, physiological, cellular, tissue, and whole plant level, which might manifest in terms of improved crop productivity. <sentence_start/>Recent advances in various disciplines of biological sciences such as metabolomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, etc., have assisted in the characterization of metabolites, transcription factors, and stress-inducible proteins involved in heavy metal tolerance, which in turn can be utilized for generating heavy metal-tolerant crops. <sentence_start/>This review summarizes various tolerance strategies of plants under heavy metal toxicity covering the role of metabolites (metabolomics), trace elements (ionomics), transcription factors (transcriptomics), various stress-inducible proteins (proteomics) as well as the role of plant hormones. <sentence_start/>We also provide a glance of some strategies adopted by metal-accumulating plants, also known as “metallophytes.<sentence_start/>”
Introduction

During the last few decades, increased anthropogenic activities, rapid industrialization, and modern agricultural practices have resulted in increased heavy metal contamination in the environment, which causes toxicity to the living organisms (Eapen and D'souza, <citation rid="B98" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.biotechadv.2004.10.001" pmid="15694122" count="1">2005</citation>; Kavamura and Esposito, <citation rid="B196" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.biotechadv.2009.09.002" pmid="19778598" count="1">2010</citation>; Miransari, <citation rid="B277" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.biotechadv.2011.04.006" pmid="21557996" count="1">2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>Large areas of land have been contaminated with heavy metals due to the use of pesticides, fertilizers, municipal and compost wastes, and also due to heavy metal release from smelting industries and metalliferous mines (Yang et al., <citation rid="B459" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jtemb.2005.02.007" pmid="16028496" count="1">2005</citation>). <sentence_start/>Although many heavy metals occur naturally in the earth's crust at various levels, the problem arises when they are released in excess into the environment due to natural and/or anthropogenic activities. <sentence_start/>The 53 elements belonging to the d-block have been categorized as “heavy metals” based on their density (>5 g/cm<sup>3</sup>) (Jarup, <citation rid="B189" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/bmb/ldg032" pmid="14757716" count="1">2003</citation>). <sentence_start/>During evolution of angiosperms, only 19 elements such as C, O, H, Mg, S, N, Ca, P, and K (macronutrients) and Cu, Zn, Mn, Fe, Mo, B, Ni, Co, Cl, and B (micronutrients) were selected for basic metabolism (Ernst, <citation rid="B104" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2006</citation>). <sentence_start/>In addition, Si is also considered as a beneficial element, and it has been reported to be involved in the maintenance of plant structures in some plants (Epstein, <citation rid="B103" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1146/annurev.arplant.50.1.641" pmid="15012222" count="1">1999</citation>). <sentence_start/>Macro and micronutrients play an important role in physiological and biochemical processes of plants such as chlorophyll biosynthesis, photosynthesis, DNA synthesis, protein modifications, redox reactions in the chloroplast and the mitochondrion, sugar metabolism, and nitrogen fixation. <sentence_start/>For example, Zn is a cofactor for more than 300 enzymes and 200 transcription factors associated with the maintenance of membrane integrity, auxin metabolism, and reproduction (Marschner, <citation rid="B259" ref-type="bibr" count="1">1995</citation>; Barker and Pilbeam, <citation rid="B32" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2007</citation>; Briat et al., <citation rid="B48" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.pbi.2007.04.003" pmid="17434791" count="1">2007</citation>; Williams and Pittman, <citation rid="B442" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2010</citation>; Prasad, <citation rid="B321" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jtemb.2012.04.004" pmid="22664333" count="1">2012</citation>; Ricachenevsky et al., <citation rid="B332" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fpls.2013.00144" pmid="23717323" pmcid="PMC3653063" count="1">2013</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, at elevated concentrations, heavy metals produce severe toxicity symptoms in plants, and therefore, their uptake and utilization are tightly controlled by the plant cells (Janicka-Russak et al., <citation rid="B188" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jxb/ern219" pmid="18820260" pmcid="PMC2561156" count="1">2008</citation>; Saito et al., <citation rid="B339" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1365-3040.2009.02068.x" pmid="19906154" count="1">2010</citation>; Singh et al., <citation rid="B382" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.plaphy.2012.09.005" pmid="23063802" count="1">2012</citation>; Srivastava et al., <citation rid="B391" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s12011-012-9406-9" pmid="22528776" count="1">2012</citation>; DalCorso et al., <citation rid="B83" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1039/c3mt00038a" pmid="23739766" count="1">2013a</citation>; Farias et al., <citation rid="B109" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/fes3.16" count="1">2013</citation>; Fidalgo et al., <citation rid="B115" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/fes3.20" count="1">2013</citation>). <sentence_start/>Some heavy metals, such as Cd, Cr, Pb, Al, Hg, etc., although being non-essential and without physiological function, are very toxic even at very low concentrations (Ernst et al., <citation rid="B105" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1365-3040.2007.01746.x" pmid="17999660" count="1">2008</citation>; Janicka-Russak et al., <citation rid="B188" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jxb/ern219" pmid="18820260" pmcid="PMC2561156" count="1">2008</citation>; Garzón et al., <citation rid="B136" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.plantsci.2011.01.022" pmid="21421422" count="1">2011</citation>; Hayat et al., <citation rid="B161" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00709-011-0331-0" pmid="22002742" count="1">2012</citation>; Shahid et al., <citation rid="B356" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jhazmat.2012.01.060" pmid="22502897" count="1">2012</citation>; Chong-qing et al., <citation rid="B70" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S1672-6308(13)60124-9" count="1">2013</citation>; Gill et al., <citation rid="B139" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.plaphy.2012.12.001" pmid="23313792" count="1">2013</citation>). <sentence_start/>Essential and non-essential heavy metals generally produce common toxic effects on plants, such as low biomass accumulation, chlorosis, inhibition of growth and photosynthesis, altered water balance and nutrient assimilation, and senescence, which ultimately cause plant death.

In addition to adverse impacts on plants, heavy metals pose threat to human health due to their persistence in nature. <sentence_start/>For instance, Pb is one of the most toxic heavy metals that has soil retention time of 150-5000 years and reported to maintain its concentration high for as long as 150 years (NandaKumar et al., <citation rid="B299" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/es00005a014" pmid="22192016" count="1">1995</citation>; Yang et al., <citation rid="B459" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jtemb.2005.02.007" pmid="16028496" count="1">2005</citation>). <sentence_start/>Plants growing in heavy metal-contaminated sites generally accumulate higher amounts of heavy metals, and thus, contamination of food chain occurs. <sentence_start/>Contaminated food chain acts as a primary route for the entry of heavy metals into animal and human tissues, making them prone to several diseases that range from dermatitis to various types of cancers (McLaughlin et al., <citation rid="B265" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S0378-4290(98)00137-3" count="1">1999</citation>). <sentence_start/>This problem might become even worse if sufficient measures are not taken at the right time. <sentence_start/>Therefore, research in this area is driven by the hope to decrease the entry of heavy metals in crop plants, thereby reducing the risk of contamination in animals and human beings.

Abiotic stresses are estimated to be the main cause for global crop yield reduction of ca. 70%, and thus, are considered a great constraint to crop production (Acquaah, <citation rid="B2" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2007</citation>; Jewell et al., <citation rid="B190" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/978-3-642-04812-8_2" count="1">2010</citation>). <sentence_start/>This situation has worsened due to disturbed equilibrium between crop productivity and population growth. <sentence_start/>Therefore, it is especially important to understand plants' responses to such stressors, particularly heavy metals, in order to find new methods for improving crops quantitatively and qualitatively. <sentence_start/>Currently, studies are being performed to address the above mentioned problems and have majorly focused on “omic” tools that take into consideration of ionomics (trace elements), metabolomics (metabolome), transcriptomics (transcriptome), and proteomics (proteome). <sentence_start/>The data obtained will provide insights that might help in enhancing stress tolerance and be employed in breeding and engineering programs aiming at developing plants with new and desired agronomical traits (Lee et al., <citation rid="B234" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jplph.2007.01.003" pmid="17360071" count="1">2007</citation>; Atkinson and Urwin, <citation rid="B26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jxb/ers100" pmid="22467407" count="1">2012</citation>). <sentence_start/>In this context, this review is focused on several aspects, from plant responses to heavy metals (considering sensitive as well as metallophytes) to the role of ionomics, metabolomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics in the regulation of heavy metal tolerance (Figure 1).
Figure 1

<bold>Integrated approach to study plant responses to heavy metal stress</bold>. <sentence_start/>Transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, and ionomics are useful tools that can help us to decipher and analyze active regulatory networks controlling heavy metal stress responses and tolerance.
Plant responses to heavy metal stress

Being sessile organisms, plants cannot escape unwanted changes in the environment. <sentence_start/>Exposure to heavy metals triggers a wide range of physiological and biochemical alterations, and plants have to develop and/or adopt a series of strategies that allow them to cope with the negative consequences of heavy metal toxicity. <sentence_start/>Plants respond to external stimuli including heavy metal toxicity <italic toggle="yes">via</italic> several mechanisms. <sentence_start/>These include (i) sensing of external stress stimuli, (ii) signal transduction and transmission of a signal into the cell, and (iii) triggering appropriate measures to counterbalance the negative effects of stress stimuli by modulating the physiological, biochemical, and molecular status of the cell. <sentence_start/>At the whole plant level, it is difficult to measure sensing and changes in the signal transduction after exposing plants to heavy metal stress. <sentence_start/>However, monitoring early responses, such as oxidative stress, transcriptomic and proteomic changes, or accumulation of metabolites, might be useful to study sensing and signal transduction changes that take place after plants' exposure to stress. <sentence_start/>For instance, Tamás et al. (<citation rid="B401" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00425-009-1042-z" pmid="19898864" count="1">2010</citation>) reported that early signs of metal toxicity in barley were similar to water deficiency signs, and thus, overexpression of genes related to dehydration stress in barley was found after exposure to Cd and Hg. <sentence_start/>Similar to this, Hernandez et al. (<citation rid="B167" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/978-3-642-22081-4_2" count="1">2012</citation>) reported oxidative stress and glutathione depletion in alfalfa roots as early signs of sensing and signal transduction after exposure to heavy metals. <sentence_start/>In another study by Zhang et al. (<citation rid="B475" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S0092-8674(02)00805-X" pmid="12110182" count="1">2002</citation>), seed germination and seedling growth of wheat was found to be inhibited due to high concentration of As. <sentence_start/>Similarly, Imran et al. (<citation rid="B180" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5897/IJPS2013.3894" count="1">2013</citation>) reported reduction in plumule and radicle length of <italic toggle="yes">Helainthus annuus</italic> L. seedlings when exposed to As. <sentence_start/>In addition, As has also been reported to decrease the photosynthetic pigment, damage chloroplast membrane, and decrease enzyme activity by reacting with the sulfhydryl group of proteins and also reported to alter nutrient balance and protein metabolism (Li et al., <citation rid="B237" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.chemosphere.2005.04.055" pmid="15972226" count="1">2006</citation>; Singh et al., <citation rid="B379" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.envpol.2009.03.036" pmid="19406540" count="1">2009</citation>; Ahsan et al., <citation rid="B5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.chemosphere.2009.11.004" pmid="19948354" count="1">2010</citation>).

Heavy metals exert toxicities in plants through four proposed mechanisms. <sentence_start/>These include (i) similarities with the nutrient cations, which result into a competition for absorption at root surface; for example, As and Cd compete with P and Zn, respectively, for their absorption; (ii) direct interaction of heavy metals with sulfhydryl group (-SH) of functional proteins, which disrupts their structure and function, and thus, renders them inactive; (iii) displacement of essential cations from specific binding sites that lead to a collapse of function; and (iv) generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which consequently damages the macromolecules (Sharma and Dietz, <citation rid="B365" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.tplants.2008.10.007" pmid="19070530" count="1">2009</citation>; DalCorso et al., <citation rid="B83" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1039/c3mt00038a" pmid="23739766" count="1">2013a</citation>).

The roots of sessile plants are the first organ that encounters heavy metals, and thus, roots have been widely studied to assess the impact of a stressor. <sentence_start/>Plants growing on heavy metal-rich soils suffer from both decreased growth and yield (Keunen et al., <citation rid="B199" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijms12106894" pmid="22072926" pmcid="PMC3211017" count="1">2011</citation>), indicating an implication of heavy metal toxicity in hampering the overall growth performance of the stressed plants (Kikui et al., <citation rid="B206" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jinorgbio.2005.06.031" pmid="16095709" count="1">2005</citation>; Panda et al., <citation rid="B306" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4161/psb.4.7.8903" pmid="19820334" pmcid="PMC2710549" count="1">2009</citation>; Buendía-González et al., <citation rid="B49" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.biortech.2010.03.027" pmid="20347590" count="1">2010</citation>; Gangwar et al., <citation rid="B133" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.scienta.2010.08.013" count="1">2010</citation>, <citation rid="B134" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11738-010-0672-x" count="1">2011</citation>; Gangwar and Singh, <citation rid="B132" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.scienta.2011.03.026" count="1">2011</citation>; Eleftheriou et al., <citation rid="B101" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00709-011-0292-3" pmid="21633932" count="1">2012</citation>; Hayat et al., <citation rid="B161" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00709-011-0331-0" pmid="22002742" count="1">2012</citation>; Silva, <citation rid="B376" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1155/2012/219462" count="1">2012</citation>; Anjum et al., <citation rid="B13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00709-014-0636-x" pmid="24682425" count="1">2014</citation>). <sentence_start/>Root growth is a combination of cell division and elongation. <sentence_start/>In this context, a decrease in mitotic activity has been reported in several plant species after exposure to heavy metals, which consequently results into a suppressed root growth (Fontes and Cox, <citation rid="B117" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/01904169809365517" count="1">1998</citation>; Doncheva et al., <citation rid="B93" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jxb/eri115" pmid="15737983" count="1">2005</citation>; Sundaramoorthy et al., <citation rid="B396" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.crvi.2010.03.002" pmid="20688280" count="1">2010</citation>; Hossain et al., <citation rid="B174" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1155/2012/872875" count="1">2012a</citation>,<citation rid="B173" ref-type="bibr" count="1">b</citation>; Thounaojam et al., <citation rid="B405" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.plaphy.2012.01.006" pmid="22306354" count="1">2012</citation>). <sentence_start/>A study by Liu et al. (<citation rid="B246" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1601-5223.1992.tb00003.x" count="1">1992</citation>) showed that Cr(VI) has greater toxic effect on cell division than Cr(III). <sentence_start/>Furthermore, Sundaramoorthy et al. (<citation rid="B396" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.crvi.2010.03.002" pmid="20688280" count="1">2010</citation>) have also observed that Cr(VI) caused an extension in cell cycle that leads to the inhibition in cell division, thereby reducing root growth.

Pena et al. (<citation rid="B312" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.plantsci.2012.07.008" pmid="23017894" count="1">2012</citation>) have reported that Cd toxicity affects the cell cycle G1/S transition and progression through S phase <italic toggle="yes">via</italic> decreased expression of a cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK), suggesting that ROS might be involved in such alterations. <sentence_start/>Yuan et al. (<citation rid="B463" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/pcp/pct030" pmid="23396597" count="1">2013</citation>) have reported that excess Cu affects both elongation and meristem zones by altering auxin distribution through PINFORMED1 (PIN1) protein, and that Cu-mediated auxin redistribution is responsible for Cu-mediated inhibition of primary root elongation. <sentence_start/>Similarly, Petö et al. (<citation rid="B315" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/aob/mcr176" pmid="21856638" pmcid="PMC3158692" count="1">2011</citation>) have also demonstrated that excess Cu inhibits root length and alters morphology by inducing alterations in auxin levels, which antagonizes nitric oxide function. <sentence_start/>It has also been demonstrated that inhibition in root growth is accompanied by an increase in root diameter, suggesting that plant cytoskeleton might also be a target of heavy metal toxicity (Zobel et al., <citation rid="B487" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11104-007-9341-2" count="1">2007</citation>). <sentence_start/>Therefore, these studies suggest that heavy metals might cause an inhibition in root growth that alters water balance and nutrient absorption, thereby affecting their transportation to the aboveground plant parts and thus negatively affecting shoot growth and ultimately decreasing biomass accumulation. <sentence_start/>Roots utilize several mechanisms such as synthesis and deposition of callose to reduce and/or avoid heavy metal toxicity. <sentence_start/>These mechanisms create a barrier for the entry of heavy metals and enhance plasticity of root anatomy. <sentence_start/>Apart from barricading the entry of heavy metals, roots also allow their transportation to aboveground plant parts (in the case of metallophytes or hyperaccumulator plants: plants that can grow in heavy metal-contaminated soil; Fahr et al., <citation rid="B107" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fpls.2013.00175" pmid="23750165" pmcid="PMC3674728" count="1">2013</citation>) for sequestration into the vacuoles rendering them inactive, and thus non-reactive.

Plasma membranes serve as a highly regulated checkpoint for an entry of unwanted substances inside the cell and protect the cell from negative consequences of many stressors. <sentence_start/>It has been reported that <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis halleri</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis arenosa</italic> were more tolerant to heavy metal stress than <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis thaliana</italic> due to the lowest membrane depolarization, indicating that rapid membrane voltage changes might be an excellent tool for monitoring the effects of heavy metal toxicity (Kenderešová et al., <citation rid="B197" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/aob/mcs111" pmid="22645116" pmcid="PMC3394654" count="1">2012</citation>). <sentence_start/>Once inside the cell, heavy metals alter metabolism that results into a reduction of growth and lower biomass accumulation (Nagajyoti et al., <citation rid="B293" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10311-010-0297-8" count="1">2010</citation>). <sentence_start/>Heavy metal toxicity might also cause stunted stem and root length, and chlorosis in younger leaves that can extend to the older leaves after prolonged exposure (Israr et al., <citation rid="B184" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.chemosphere.2006.02.016" pmid="16564071" count="1">2006</citation>; Guo et al., <citation rid="B144" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.chemosphere.2008.04.018" pmid="18504054" count="1">2008a</citation>,<citation rid="B145" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.108.115782" pmid="18287486" pmcid="PMC2287344" count="1">b</citation>; Warne et al., <citation rid="B438" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1897/07-294.1" pmid="18333681" count="1">2008</citation>; Gangwar and Singh, <citation rid="B132" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.scienta.2011.03.026" count="1">2011</citation>; Gangwar et al., <citation rid="B134" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11738-010-0672-x" count="1">2011</citation>; Srivastava et al., <citation rid="B391" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s12011-012-9406-9" pmid="22528776" count="1">2012</citation>). <sentence_start/>At the cellular and molecular levels, heavy metal toxicity affects plants in many ways. <sentence_start/>For instance, it alters the key physiological and biochemical processes such as seed germination, pigment synthesis, photosynthesis, gas exchanges, respiration, inactivation and denaturation of enzymes, blocks functional groups of metabolically important molecules, hormonal balance, nutrient assimilation, protein synthesis, and DNA replication (Nagajyoti et al., <citation rid="B293" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10311-010-0297-8" count="1">2010</citation>; Yadav, <citation rid="B455" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.sajb.2009.10.007" count="1">2010</citation>; Keunen et al., <citation rid="B199" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijms12106894" pmid="22072926" pmcid="PMC3211017" count="1">2011</citation>; He et al., <citation rid="B162" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00709-011-0310-5" pmid="21850424" count="1">2012</citation>; Hossain et al., <citation rid="B174" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1155/2012/872875" count="1">2012a</citation>,<citation rid="B173" ref-type="bibr" count="1">b</citation>; Silva, <citation rid="B376" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1155/2012/219462" count="1">2012</citation>; Wani et al., <citation rid="B437" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2012</citation>; Singh et al., <citation rid="B383" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.plaphy.2013.07.003" pmid="23917073" count="1">2013</citation>). <sentence_start/>Under Cd stress, severe deleterious effects on various photosynthetic indices such as photosynthetic rate (Pn) and intracellular CO<sub>2</sub> concentration (Ci) have been reported in tomato seedlings (Dong et al., <citation rid="B94" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1631/jzus.2005.B0974" pmid="16187410" pmcid="PMC1390439" count="1">2005</citation>). <sentence_start/>Maleva et al. (<citation rid="B257" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1134/S1021443712020069" count="1">2012</citation>) have observed that Mn, Cu, Cd, Zn, and Ni caused a significant decline in the levels of chlorophyll contents, accompanied by a decrease in the photochemical efficiency of photosystem II (PS II) in <italic toggle="yes">Elodea densa</italic>. <sentence_start/>Similarly, Li et al. (<citation rid="B235" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s13131-012-0210-3" count="1">2012</citation>) have also reported that Cu, Zn, Pb, and Cd depressed chlorophyll and carotenoids levels and the quantum yield of PS II in <italic toggle="yes">Thalassia hemprichii</italic>, indicating that heavy metals have negative consequences on photosynthesis. <sentence_start/>Apart from affecting light reactions, heavy metals decrease CO<sub>2</sub> assimilation by either diminishing RUBP carboxylase activity or by reacting with the thiol group of RUBISCO. <sentence_start/>For instance, Zn has been reported to inhibit RUBISCO activity in <italic toggle="yes">Phaseolus vulgaris</italic> by replacing Zn<sup>+2</sup> for Mg<sup>+2</sup>, as both are bivalent cations (Monnet et al., <citation rid="B284" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1078/S0176-1617(04)70140-6" count="1">2001</citation>). <sentence_start/>In another study on <italic toggle="yes">Erythrina variegate</italic> by Muthuchelian et al. (<citation rid="B291" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1078/0176-1617-00627" count="1">2001</citation>), decreased RUBISCO activity was observed under Cd stress, and this decrease in RUBISCO activity might be due to the formation of mercaptide by Cd with thiol group of RUBISCO (Siborova, <citation rid="B374" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S0015-3796(88)80045-3" count="1">1988</citation>). <sentence_start/>These researchers also reported decreased CO<sub>2</sub> fixation, which is possibly due to a decrease in ATP and reductant pool (Husaini and Rai, <citation rid="B178" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S0176-1617(11)80518-3" count="1">1991</citation>), as Cd ions decrease the proton source for reduction reactions (Ferretti et al., <citation rid="B114" ref-type="bibr" count="1">1993</citation>). <sentence_start/>Similarly, Cu, a well-known inhibitor of carboxylase and oxygenase activities of RUBISCO (Lidon and Henriques, <citation rid="B241" ref-type="bibr" count="1">1991</citation>), was found to decrease RUBISCO activity in <italic toggle="yes">Chenopodium rubrum</italic> (Schafer et al., <citation rid="B350" ref-type="bibr" count="1">1992</citation>) by interacting with the essential cysteine residue of the enzyme (Siborova, <citation rid="B374" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S0015-3796(88)80045-3" count="1">1988</citation>). <sentence_start/>Such reduction in pigments, photosynthetic rate, quantum yield of PS II, gas exchange, stomatal conductance, and CO<sub>2</sub> assimilation might be linked to the ultrastructural changes (changes at cellular and tissue levels) induced by heavy metal stress. <sentence_start/>The effects arising due to changes in ultrastructures of membranes have been reported in several studies (Azzarello et al., <citation rid="B28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.envexpbot.2012.02.008" count="1">2012</citation>; Basile et al., <citation rid="B34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.envpol.2012.03.018" pmid="22516710" count="1">2012</citation>; Esposito et al., <citation rid="B106" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/15226514.2011.620904" pmid="22567723" count="1">2012</citation>; He et al., <citation rid="B162" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00709-011-0310-5" pmid="21850424" count="1">2012</citation>; Sánchez-Pardo et al., <citation rid="B344" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.envexpbot.2012.04.017" count="1">2012</citation>; Ali et al., <citation rid="B10" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10535-013-0358-5" count="1">2013a</citation>,<citation rid="B11" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00344-013-9328-6" count="1">b</citation>). <sentence_start/>Moreover, heavy metals have been reported to affect another key physiological process, i.e., nitrogen metabolism, which is involved in plant function, from metabolism to allocation of resources, thereby regulating plant growth and development. <sentence_start/>Heavy metals have been found to enhance protease activity (Chaffei et al., <citation rid="B61" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1081/PLN-120022372" count="1">2003</citation>), and thus, reducing the activity of enzymes involved in nitrate (Nitrate reductase; NR and Nitrite reductase; NiR) and ammonia (Glutamine synthetase; GS, Glutamine oxoglutarate aminotransferase; GOGAT and Glutamate dehydrogenase; GDH) assimilation. <sentence_start/>The heavy metal Cd has been reported to affect nitrogen metabolism by inhibiting nitrate uptake and transportation, nitrate reductase, and GS activity (Hernández et al., <citation rid="B166" ref-type="bibr" count="1">1997</citation>; Lea and Miflin, <citation rid="B229" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S0981-9428(03)00060-3" count="1">2004</citation>), thereby affecting primary N assimilation processes.

Heavy metal-mediated alteration in hormonal balance correlates with their toxicities in plants (Petö et al., <citation rid="B315" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/aob/mcr176" pmid="21856638" pmcid="PMC3158692" count="1">2011</citation>; Wilkinson et al., <citation rid="B441" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jxb/ers148" pmid="22641615" count="1">2012</citation>). <sentence_start/>For instance, in <italic toggle="yes">Brassica juncea</italic>, As causes toxicity by changing the levels of the auxins:indole-3-acetic acid (IAA), indole-3- butyric acid (IBA), and naphthalene acetic acid (NAA) and altering the expression of about 69 microRNAs (Srivastava et al., <citation rid="B392" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jxb/ers333" pmid="23162117" count="1">2013</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, exogenous supply of IAA improves the growth of <italic toggle="yes">B. juncea</italic> under As stress, suggesting an implication of the regulation of the hormone level in the management of As stress.
Metallophytes under heavy metal stress

Metallophytes, also known as hyperaccumulators, have the ability to uptake large amounts of heavy metals from the soil, and this property makes them unique to be utilized in technologies such as biogeochemical and biogeobotanical prospection and phytoremediation. <sentence_start/>The absorbed heavy metals from the soil by these hyperaccumulators are not retained in the roots but are translocated to the shoots and accumulated in the aboveground organs at concentrations 100-1000-fold higher than the observed in non-hyperaccumulating species (Figures 2ia,b). <sentence_start/>However, this high concentration does not pose any toxic effect on plants (Rascio, <citation rid="B327" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2307/3543610" count="1">1997</citation>; Reeves, <citation rid="B331" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2006</citation>; Prasad et al., <citation rid="B322" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.envpol.2009.07.038" pmid="19683373" count="1">2010</citation>). <sentence_start/>With significant advances in our understanding of the mechanisms adopted by hyperaccumulators, there has been implication of three hallmarks that distinguish them from non-hyperaccumultors. <sentence_start/>These are (i) greater capability of heavy metal uptake, (ii) root-to-shoot translocation of heavy metal, and (iii) detoxification and sequestration of heavy metal (Figures 2iia-c). <sentence_start/>Studies on <italic toggle="yes">Thlaspi caerulescens</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">A. halleri</italic>, model plants for studying heavy metal tolerance strategies, have been done (Milner and Kochian, <citation rid="B275" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/aob/mcn063" pmid="18440996" pmcid="PMC2712422" count="1">2008</citation>; Singh et al., <citation rid="B379" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.envpol.2009.03.036" pmid="19406540" count="1">2009</citation>; Frérot et al., <citation rid="B125" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8137.2010.03295.x" pmid="20487314" count="1">2010</citation>; Krämer, <citation rid="B214" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1146/annurev-arplant-042809-112156" pmid="20192749" count="1">2010</citation>). <sentence_start/>The studies have revealed that hyperaccumulation is not due to the presence of a novel gene, but it arises only from differential expression of genes that are common to hyperaccumulators and non-hyperaccumulators (Verbruggen et al., <citation rid="B423" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8137.2008.02748.x" pmid="19192189" count="1">2009</citation>). <sentence_start/>Hyperaccumulation of heavy metal includes three complex phenomena discussed below:

Heavy metal uptake

Hyperaccumulators have an extraordinary ability to absorb heavy metals from the soil under varying concentration of heavy metals (Ma et al., <citation rid="B256" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/35054664" pmid="11214308" count="1">2001</citation>; Yang et al., <citation rid="B458" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2002</citation>). <sentence_start/>Although heavy metals are taken up by hyperaccumulators, their uptake is affected by several factors such as pH, water content, organic substances, etc. <sentence_start/>Moreover, heavy metal uptake requires a suitable transporting system to enter the plant (Figure 2i). <sentence_start/>Several researchers have reported that pH affects (i) proton secretion by roots that further acidify rhizosphere, thus enhancing metal dissolution, and (ii) the growth of metal-accumulating plant species (Bernal et al., <citation rid="B41" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/BF00010077" count="1">1994</citation>; Peng et al., <citation rid="B314" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1081/ESE-200048283" pmid="15792303" count="1">2005</citation>; Kuriakose and Prasad, <citation rid="B221" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10725-007-9237-4" count="1">2008</citation>). <sentence_start/>Apart from pH, organic substances released from the roots affect growth in hyperaccumulating plants. <sentence_start/>Krishnamurti et al. (<citation rid="B219" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2134/jeq1997.00472425002600010038x" count="1">1997</citation>) have reported that organic acids released influence Cd solubility by forming Cd complexes. <sentence_start/>Therefore, pH and organic substances released from the rhizosphere of a hyperaccumulator mobilize heavy metal and enhance absorption (Krishnamurti et al., <citation rid="B219" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2134/jeq1997.00472425002600010038x" count="1">1997</citation>; Peng et al., <citation rid="B314" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1081/ESE-200048283" pmid="15792303" count="1">2005</citation>). <sentence_start/>High uptake of heavy metal has also been associated with enhanced root proliferation (Whiting et al., <citation rid="B440" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1046/j.1469-8137.2000.00570.x" count="1">2000</citation>). <sentence_start/>Furthermore, constitutive overexpression of genes also attributes to enhanced heavy metal uptake. <sentence_start/>To pinpoint the genes involved in overexpression, several comparative studies have been performed in hyperaccumulating <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis halleri</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">Thlapsi caerulescens</italic> with that of congener non-hyperaccumulating species. <sentence_start/>Studies on <italic toggle="yes">T. caerulescens</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">A. halleri</italic> have revealed that increased Zn uptake is due to overexpression of genes belonging to the ZIP (Zinc-regulated transporter Iron-regulated transporter proteins) family encoding plasma membrane located transporters (Assunção et al., <citation rid="B22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1365-3040.2001.00666.x" count="1">2001</citation>): ZTN1 and ZTN2 in <italic toggle="yes">T. caerulescens</italic> and ZIP6 and ZIP9 in <italic toggle="yes">A. halleri</italic>. <sentence_start/>The decreased uptake of Cd under increasing Zn concentration was noticed in both genera, and it clearly demonstrated that expression of ZIP genes is Zn regulated (Assunção et al., <citation rid="B23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.1004788107" pmid="20479230" pmcid="PMC2890486" count="1">2010</citation>) and Cd influx is mainly due to Zn transporters having strong preference for Zn over Cd (Weber et al., <citation rid="B439" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1365-3040.2005.01479.x" pmid="17087478" count="1">2006</citation>). <sentence_start/>Evidence exists that As being a chemical analog of phosphate enters the plant cell <italic toggle="yes">via</italic> phosphate transporters (Meharg and Hartley-Whitaker, <citation rid="B266" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1046/j.1469-8137.2002.00363.x" count="1">2002</citation>; Kanoun-Boulé et al., <citation rid="B195" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.aquatox.2008.09.009" pmid="19027182" count="1">2009</citation>). <sentence_start/>Similarly, a study on the As hyperaccumulator <italic toggle="yes">Pteris vittata</italic> and non-hyperaccumulator <italic toggle="yes">Pteris tremula</italic> has shown that plasma membranes of root cells of <italic toggle="yes">P. vittata</italic> had high density of phosphate/arsenate transporters than <italic toggle="yes">P. tremula</italic> (Caille et al., <citation rid="B51" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8137.2004.01239.x" pmid="15720686" count="1">2005</citation>), possibly due to constitutive gene overexpression. <sentence_start/>In addition, a study on the Se hyperaccumulators <italic toggle="yes">Astragalus bisulcatus</italic> (Fabaceae) and <italic toggle="yes">Stanleya pinnata</italic> (Brassicaceae) revealed that there was a higher Se/S ratio in the shoots of these species in comparison to the non-hyperaccumulator sister species, and this observation also supported the fact that an enhanced Se uptake was through sulfate transporters (Galeas et al., <citation rid="B131" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8137.2006.01943.x" pmid="17244046" count="1">2007</citation>).
Root-to-shoot translocation of heavy metals

Unlike non-hyperaccumulator plants, hyperaccumulators do not retain the heavy metal absorbed from roots but translocate them into shoots <italic toggle="yes">via</italic> xylem and several classes of proteins are involved in this translocation. <sentence_start/>The proteins involved are heavy metal-transporting ATPases (or CPx-type, P1B-type), natural resistance-associated macrophage proteins (Nramp), cation diffusion facilitator (CDF) family proteins, zinc-iron permease (ZIP) family proteins, and MATE (Multidrug And Toxin Efflux) protein family. <sentence_start/>The CPx-type ATPases are involved in transporting toxic metals like Cu, Zn, Cd, and Pb using ATP across cell membranes (Williams et al., <citation rid="B443" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S0005-2736(00)00133-4" pmid="10748249" count="1">2000</citation>). <sentence_start/>The P1B-type ATPases also have the similar role of transporting heavy metal, but they also regulate metal homeostasis as well as tolerance (Axelsen and Palmgren, <citation rid="B27" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/PL00006286" pmid="9419228" count="1">1998</citation>). <sentence_start/>These heavy metal ATPases (HMAs) overexpressed in roots and shoots of hyperaccumulators suggest their upregulation in hyperaccumulators in comparison to non-hyperaccumulators (Papoyan and Kochian, <citation rid="B308" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.104.044503" pmid="15516513" pmcid="PMC527178" count="1">2004</citation>). <sentence_start/>Nramp is another class of protein family that has been found to be involved in transporting heavy metal ions, and genes coding for these proteins are termed as <italic toggle="yes">Nramp</italic> genes. <sentence_start/>Studies on rice revealed three homologs of this protein, namely OsNramp1, OsNramp2, and OsNramp3, and these proteins expressed in different tissues of rice transport distinct but related ions (Belouchi et al., <citation rid="B40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1023/A:1005723304911" pmid="9154989" count="1">1997</citation>). <sentence_start/>Another class of proteins (CDF) have been found to be involved in transporting Zn, Co, and Cd, and regulate effluxing of cation out of the cytoplasmic compartment, and therefore, they are termed as “cation efflux transporters” (Mäser et al., <citation rid="B260" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.126.4.1646" pmid="11500563" pmcid="PMC117164" count="1">2001</citation>). <sentence_start/>A related Zn transporter (ZNT1) from <italic toggle="yes">T. caerulescens</italic> was reported by Pence et al. (<citation rid="B313" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.97.9.4956" pmid="10781104" pmcid="PMC18339" count="1">2000</citation>), which belongs to a superfamily known as ZIP gene family, and was found to be expressed at high levels in roots and shoots. <sentence_start/>Another Zn transporter ZAT1 was also reported in <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis</italic> that was highly expressed in root tissues (van der Zaal et al., <citation rid="B419" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.119.3.1047" pmid="10069843" pmcid="PMC32086" count="1">1999</citation>). <sentence_start/>The transporter protein MATE is also involved in heavy metal translocation; FDR3, a protein of this family, was found to be expressed in roots of <italic toggle="yes">T. caerulescens</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">A. halleri</italic>, and the gene encoding this protein FDR3 plays a role in translocation of heavy metal (Talke et al., <citation rid="B400" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.105.076232" pmid="16844841" pmcid="PMC1557598" count="1">2006</citation>; van de Mortel et al., <citation rid="B418" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.106.082073" pmid="16998091" pmcid="PMC1630723" count="1">2006</citation>; Krämer et al., <citation rid="B217" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.febslet.2007.04.010" pmid="17462635" count="1">2007</citation>). <sentence_start/>Therefore, the abovementioned studies provide strong evidence that multiple transporter proteins are involved in the translocation of heavy metal.
Detoxification/sequestration of heavy metal

After translocating, hyperaccumulators sequestrate and then detoxify the heavy metal, a process that allows them to survive under metal-contaminated areas without suffering from any toxic effect (Figure 2ii). <sentence_start/>The process of detoxification/sequestration occurs in the vacuole of plants (Vögeli-Lange and Wagner, <citation rid="B428" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.92.4.1086" pmid="16667375" pmcid="PMC1062420" count="1">1990</citation>; Kanoun-Boulé et al., <citation rid="B195" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.aquatox.2008.09.009" pmid="19027182" count="1">2009</citation>; Singh et al., <citation rid="B380" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00709-010-0249-y" pmid="21161305" count="1">2011a</citation>) and several transporter families are involved in this process, namelyABC, CDF, HMA, and NRAMP transporters. <sentence_start/>The ABC transporters are involved in transporting heavy metal into the vacuole and mainly two subfamilies (MRP and PDR) are active. <sentence_start/>The HMT1, first vacuolar ABC transporter reported in <italic toggle="yes">Schizosaccharomyces pombe</italic>, localized in the tonoplast aids in transporting PC-Cd (phytochelatins-cadmium) complexes formed in the cytosol (Ortiz et al., <citation rid="B303" ref-type="bibr" pmid="1396551" doi="10.1002/j.1460-2075.1992.tb05431.x" pmcid="PMC556806" count="1">1992</citation>, <citation rid="B304" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1074/jbc.270.9.4721" pmid="7876244" count="1">1995</citation>; Kuriakose and Prasad, <citation rid="B221" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10725-007-9237-4" count="1">2008</citation>). <sentence_start/>Later on, a functional homolog of HMT1 has been reported in <italic toggle="yes">Caenorhabditis elegans</italic> and Drosophila (Vatamaniuk et al., <citation rid="B422" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1074/jbc.M503362200" pmid="15840570" count="1">2005</citation>; Sooksa-Nguan et al., <citation rid="B390" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1074/jbc.M806501200" pmid="19001374" count="1">2009</citation>); however, no such homolog was studied in plants. <sentence_start/>Studies in <italic toggle="yes">A. thaliana</italic> have revealed two transporters AtMRP1 and AtMRP2 in transporting PC-Cd complexes into the vacuole (Lu et al., <citation rid="B252" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.94.15.8243" pmid="9223346" pmcid="PMC21588" count="1">1997</citation>, <citation rid="B253" ref-type="bibr" pmid="9490749" doi="10.1105/tpc.10.2.267" pmcid="PMC143980" count="1">1998</citation>), and these transporters confer the metal tolerance. <sentence_start/>The CDF transporter family, also named “metal tolerance protein (MTP),” is also involved in transporting metal cations such as Zn<sup>2+</sup>, Cd<sup>2+</sup>, Co<sup>2+</sup>, Ni<sup>2+</sup>, or Mn<sup>2+</sup> from the cytosol to the vacuole (Krämer et al., <citation rid="B217" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.febslet.2007.04.010" pmid="17462635" count="1">2007</citation>; Montanini et al., <citation rid="B285" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/1471-2164-8-107" pmid="17448255" pmcid="PMC1868760" count="1">2007</citation>). <sentence_start/>They have been categorized into two of four distinct groups of which groups I and III are the most important (Blaudez et al., <citation rid="B44" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1105/tpc.017541" pmid="14630973" pmcid="PMC282827" count="1">2003</citation>). <sentence_start/>Comparative studies in <italic toggle="yes">A. halleri</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">T. caerulescens</italic> with those of non-hyperaccumulators have shown higher expression of MTP1 (group III), MTP8 (group I), and MTP11 (group I) (Becher et al., <citation rid="B37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1046/j.1365-313X.2003.01959.x" pmid="14690509" count="1">2004</citation>; Talke et al., <citation rid="B400" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.105.076232" pmid="16844841" pmcid="PMC1557598" count="1">2006</citation>; van de Mortel et al., <citation rid="B418" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.106.082073" pmid="16998091" pmcid="PMC1630723" count="1">2006</citation>). <sentence_start/>Similarly, AhMTP1 protein also showed a constitutive higher expression in leaves of <italic toggle="yes">A. halleri</italic> under exogenous supply of Zn (Dräger et al., <citation rid="B95" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1365-313X.2004.02143.x" pmid="15255871" count="1">2004</citation>). <sentence_start/>The MTP11 and MTP8 were found to be close homologs of ShMTP8 (formerly ShMTP1) and confirmed Mn tolerance in <italic toggle="yes">A. thaliana</italic> (Delhaize et al., <citation rid="B87" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1105/tpc.009134" pmid="12724539" pmcid="PMC153721" count="1">2003</citation>), thus suggesting a role of these proteins in metal tolerance. <sentence_start/>Likewise, other transporter proteins such as HMA and NRAMP are also involved in transporting the metal from the cytosol to the vacuole. <sentence_start/>However, HMAs are thought to be involved in detoxification mechanisms due to their overexpression, as reported in <italic toggle="yes">A. thaliana</italic> (Morel et al., <citation rid="B286" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.108.130294" pmid="19036834" pmcid="PMC2633814" count="1">2009</citation>).

Apart from the role of transporter proteins, organic acids are also involved in detoxification mechanisms, as they help in entrapping the metal ion and chelating them. <sentence_start/>For instance, citrate binds with Ni in leaves of <italic toggle="yes">Thlaspi goesingense</italic>, enabling formation of metal-organic acid complex for chelation (Krämer et al., <citation rid="B216" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.122.4.1343" pmid="10759531" pmcid="PMC58970" count="1">2000</citation>). <sentence_start/>Similarly, malate binds with Zn in <italic toggle="yes">A. halleri</italic> and Cd in <italic toggle="yes">T. caerulescens</italic> (Salt et al., <citation rid="B342" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/es980825x" count="1">1999</citation>; Sarret et al., <citation rid="B347" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.007799" pmid="12481065" pmcid="PMC166693" count="1">2002</citation>). <sentence_start/>The role of amino acids in hyperaccumulator has been found to be important due to the formation of stable complexes with bivalent cations (Callahan et al., <citation rid="B54" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00775-005-0056-7" pmid="16328457" count="1">2006</citation>), thus helping largely in sequestrating metal cations. <sentence_start/>For example, histidine (His) is involved in Ni hyperaccumulation, and a high concentration of His has been reported in the roots of Ni hyperaccumulators (Assuncão et al., <citation rid="B21" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1046/j.1469-8137.2003.00820.x" pmid="33873356" count="1">2003</citation>). <sentence_start/>The mechanism of heavy metal detoxification in hyperaccumulators also relies on the overexpression of genes related with antioxidant activity such as reduced glutathione (GSH), cysteine and <italic toggle="yes">O</italic>-acetylserine (Anjum et al., <citation rid="B13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00709-014-0636-x" pmid="24682425" count="1">2014</citation>). <sentence_start/>Studies have revealed that upstream signaling of salicylic acid results in increased serine acetyltransferase (SAT) activity and higher GSH level (Freeman et al., <citation rid="B122" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.104.055293" pmid="15734913" pmcid="PMC1065408" count="1">2005a</citation>). <sentence_start/>Similarly, overexpression of <italic toggle="yes">NgSAT</italic> in <italic toggle="yes">Noccaea goesingense</italic> resulted in enhanced levels of GSH that resulted in Ni, Co, Zn, and to a small extent Cd tolerance (Freeman et al., <citation rid="B123" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1105/tpc.104.023036" pmid="15269333" pmcid="PMC519206" count="1">2004</citation>; Freeman and Salt, <citation rid="B121" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/1471-2229-7-63" pmid="18045473" pmcid="PMC2233625" count="1">2007</citation>).
Heavy metal and reactive oxygen species (ROS) production

Another negative consequence of heavy metal accumulation is the generation of ROS. <sentence_start/>In plants, ROS accumulation depends upon the balance between ROS production and ROS scavenging (Mittler et al., <citation rid="B281" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.tplants.2004.08.009" pmid="15465684" count="1">2004</citation>), which in turn also depends on growth conditions such as temperature, light intensity, presence of heavy metal, etc. <sentence_start/>For instance, the presence of excess heavy metals results into a limitation of CO<sub>2</sub> fixation in the chloroplasts, which coupled with an over reduction of the photosynthetic electron transport chain serves as a major site of ROS production (Mittler et al., <citation rid="B281" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.tplants.2004.08.009" pmid="15465684" count="1">2004</citation>). <sentence_start/>Over reduction of the electron transport chains in the mitochondria is also a major site of ROS generation (Davidson and Schiestl, <citation rid="B84" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1128/MCB.21.24.8483-8489.2001" pmid="11713283" pmcid="PMC100011" count="1">2001</citation>; Keunen et al., <citation rid="B199" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijms12106894" pmid="22072926" pmcid="PMC3211017" count="1">2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>Møller et al. (<citation rid="B283" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1146/annurev.arplant.58.032806.103946" pmid="17288534" count="1">2007</citation>) reported that 1-5% of O<sub>2</sub> consumed by the isolated mitochondria converts into ROS. <sentence_start/>ROS hydrogen peroxide (H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) is produced in the peroxisomes after glycolate is oxidized to glyoxylic acid during photorespiration (Mittler et al., <citation rid="B281" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.tplants.2004.08.009" pmid="15465684" count="1">2004</citation>). <sentence_start/>Therefore, ROS such as singlet oxygen (<sup>1</sup>O<sub>2</sub>), superoxide anion ( ), H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, and hydroxyl radicals (<sup>∙</sup>OH) are produced in these organelles because of spin inversion and one-two and three-electron transfer reactions to O<sub>2</sub>, respectively, during functioning of the electron transport chains (Sharma and Dietz, <citation rid="B365" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.tplants.2008.10.007" pmid="19070530" count="1">2009</citation>). <sentence_start/>The redox active heavy metals such as Cu, Cd Fe, and Zn can induce ROS formation directly by participating in Haber-Weiss and Fenton reactions or indirectly by inhibiting the functioning of enzymes in the cellular antioxidant defense network (Schützendübel and Polle, <citation rid="B353" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jexbot/53.372.1351" pmid="11997381" count="1">2002</citation>; Halliwell, <citation rid="B151" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.106.077073" pmid="16760481" pmcid="PMC1475431" count="1">2006</citation>; Keunen et al., <citation rid="B199" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijms12106894" pmid="22072926" pmcid="PMC3211017" count="1">2011</citation>).

ROS are unstable, highly reactive, and thus, promptly react with other macromolecules to generate more free radicals because unpaired electrons tend to pair and give rise to two stable electron bonds (Foyer and Halliwell, <citation rid="B119" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/BF00386001" pmid="24425174" count="1">1976</citation>). <sentence_start/>Being extremely reactive in nature, ROS can interact with macromolecules such as DNA, pigments, proteins, lipids, and other essential cellular molecules depending on the properties like chemical reactivity, redox potential, half-life, and mobility within the cellular system, ultimately leading to a series of destructive processes collectively termed as “oxidative stress” (Mittler, <citation rid="B280" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S1360-1385(02)02312-9" pmid="12234732" count="1">2002</citation>; Sharma and Dietz, <citation rid="B365" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.tplants.2008.10.007" pmid="19070530" count="1">2009</citation>; Hossain et al., <citation rid="B174" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1155/2012/872875" count="1">2012a</citation>,<citation rid="B173" ref-type="bibr" count="1">b</citation>). <sentence_start/>Among ROS, <sup>∙</sup>OH is the most reactive, highly damaging, and short-lived (1 ns), and can oxidize macromolecules within a diffusion distance. <sentence_start/>Therefore, ROS might induce reversible as well as irreversible modifications in lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids; however, most of these ROS effects are damaging and irreversible.

Conversely, ROS also act as signaling molecules involved in the regulation of many key physiological processes such as root hair growth, stomatal movement, cell growth, and cell differentiation when finely tuned and regulated by an antioxidative defense system (Foreman et al., <citation rid="B118" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nature01485" pmid="12660786" count="1">2003</citation>; Kwak et al., <citation rid="B222" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.106.079004" pmid="16760482" pmcid="PMC1475468" count="1">2006</citation>; Tsukagoshi et al., <citation rid="B413" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2010.10.020" pmid="21074051" count="1">2010</citation>). <sentence_start/>It has been shown in several studies that ROS generated by NADPH oxidases during stress are channeled by the plant to serve as a stress signal to activate acclimation and defense mechanisms, which in turn counteract oxidative stress (Mittler et al., <citation rid="B281" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.tplants.2004.08.009" pmid="15465684" count="1">2004</citation>; Davletova et al., <citation rid="B85" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1105/tpc.104.026971" pmid="15608336" pmcid="PMC544504" count="1">2005</citation>; Miller et al., <citation rid="B272" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1399-3054.2008.01090.x" pmid="18346071" count="1">2008</citation>, <citation rid="B273" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1365-3040.2009.02041.x" pmid="19712065" count="1">2010</citation>). <sentence_start/>Therefore, the fate of ROS (i.e., whether it will act as signaling molecule or damaging one) in the cellular system depends upon the output of many complex processes that involve in antioxidative system, signaling cascades, redox alterations, etc. <sentence_start/>When the generation of ROS exceeds that of the scavenging potential of antioxidants, oxidative stress occurs (Figure 3).
Figure 3

<bold>Heavy metal induced-oxidative stress, tolerance, and detoxification mechanisms in the plant cell</bold>. <sentence_start/>AsA, ascorbic acid; CAT, catalase; Cys, cysteine; c-ECS, c-glutamylcysteinesynthetase; Glu, glutamine; Gly, glycine; GR, glutathione reductase; GS, glutathione synthetase; GSH, glutathione (reduced); GSSG, oxidized glutathione; H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, hydrogen peroxide; MDHA, monodehydroascorbate; O<sub>2</sub>, oxygen molecule; , superoxide radicals; ROS, reactive oxygen species; SOD, superoxide dismutase; A, heavy metal.

Plants possess a specific mechanism to keep the routinely formed ROS at physiological limit, preventing them from exceeding toxic threshold levels, thereby playing an important role in the acclimation process against an imposed stress (Mittler et al., <citation rid="B281" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.tplants.2004.08.009" pmid="15465684" count="1">2004</citation>). <sentence_start/>This mechanism is known as the plant antioxidant defense system that regulates ROS levels in the cellular system at a particular time (Figure 3). <sentence_start/>An antioxidant system comprises two types of components: enzymatic and non-enzymatic. <sentence_start/>The enzymatic antioxidants include superoxide dismutase (SOD; EC 1.15.1.1), catalase (CAT; EC 1.11.1.6), ascorbate peroxidase (APX; EC 1.11.1.11), glutathione reductase (GR; EC 1.6.4.2), monodehydroascorbate reductase (MDHAR; EC 1.6.5.4), dehydroascorbate reductase (DHAR; EC 1.8.5.1), glutathione peroxidase (GPX; EC 1.11.1.9), and glutathione-S-transferase (GST; EC 2.5.1.18), whereas non-enzymatic antioxidants include water-soluble compounds such as ascorbate, glutathione, proline, and α-tocopherol (Apel and Hirt, <citation rid="B15" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1146/annurev.arplant.55.031903.141701" pmid="15377225" count="1">2004</citation>; Sharma and Dietz, <citation rid="B365" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.tplants.2008.10.007" pmid="19070530" count="1">2009</citation>; Hossain et al., <citation rid="B172" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11703-010-1070-2" count="1">2011</citation>, <citation rid="B174" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1155/2012/872875" count="1">2012a</citation>,<citation rid="B173" ref-type="bibr" count="1">b</citation>). <sentence_start/>Although ascorbate and glutathione both function as cofactors of enzymatic antioxidants, both can also directly quench ROS and regulate the gene expression associated with biotic and abiotic stress responses (Hossain et al., <citation rid="B174" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1155/2012/872875" count="1">2012a</citation>,<citation rid="B173" ref-type="bibr" count="1">b</citation>). <sentence_start/>The importance of antioxidants is based on the facts that their increased and/or decreased levels are generally related to an enhanced or declined stress tolerance of stressed plants. <sentence_start/>Since the evolution of O<sub>2</sub>, antioxidants play an important role in sustaining ROS concentration at an appropriate level that can promote plant development and reinforce resistance to stressors by modulating the expression of a set of genes and redox signaling pathways (Neill et al., <citation rid="B300" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S1369-5266(02)00282-0" pmid="12183176" count="1">2002</citation>). <sentence_start/>Keeping into consideration the importance of antioxidants in managing ROS levels and oxidative stress, the responses of transgenic plants and/or organisms overexpressing antioxidant and/or its biosynthetic pathway gene(s) against heavy metal stress are listed in Table 1.
Plant antioxidant defense system

The term “antioxidant” refers to a class of compounds that protect cells from damage caused by exposure to certain highly reactive species like ROS. <sentence_start/>The network and coordination of antioxidants are solely responsible for removing, neutralizing, and scavenging ROS. <sentence_start/>SOD is an enzyme involved in dismutating superoxide radicals generated by oxidation of molecular oxygen into H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>2</sub> in all the cellular compartments (Fridovich, <citation rid="B126" ref-type="bibr" pmid="2542241" count="1">1989</citation>).

H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> produced by the action of SOD is quite dangerous as it can diffuse through the membrane very easily and damage other cellular components, and thus, metabolites (ascorbate and glutathione) and enzymes (monodehydroascorbate reductase; MDHAR, dehydroascorbate reductase; DHAR and glutathione reductase; GR) are implicated in scavenging of H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>(Foyer et al., <citation rid="B120" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1399-3054.1997.tb04780.x" count="1">1997</citation>). <sentence_start/>Three types of SODs have been reported in plants on the basis of the metal containing (1) the chloroplastic or cytosolic Cu-Zn SOD; the cytosolic Cu-Zn SOD is referred to as Cu-Zn SOD I, whereas the chloroplastic one is referred to as Cu-Zn SOD II; (2) Mitochondrial Mn SOD, and (3) the chloroplastic Fe SOD. <sentence_start/>APX is regarded as a housekeeping protein in the cytosol and chloroplast, and is involved in scavenging of H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>. <sentence_start/>The substrate for this enzyme is ascorbate and the product, which is a radical, is reduced to dehydroascorbate by an enzyme MDHAR in the presence of an electron donor NADPH (Asada, <citation rid="B19" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1399-3054.1992.tb04728.x" count="1">1992</citation>, <citation rid="B20" ref-type="bibr" count="1">1996</citation>). <sentence_start/>CAT is an important oxidoreductase enzyme that catalyzes decomposition of H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> into H<sub>2</sub>O and O<sub>2</sub>, and it is found in most plants and is localized in the peroxisome. <sentence_start/>CAT is a key enzyme involved in detoxifying peroxides generated during photorespiration (Morita et al., <citation rid="B287" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.105.3.1015" pmid="8058828" pmcid="PMC160753" count="1">1994</citation>; Lin and Kao, <citation rid="B242" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1023/A:1006345126589" count="1">2000</citation>). <sentence_start/>Although APX and CAT serves the same function of detoxifying, different affinities (on the basis of Km values) of APX and CAT depict the role of APX in modulating H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> for signaling and CAT in detoxifying excess H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> during stress (Mittler, <citation rid="B280" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S1360-1385(02)02312-9" pmid="12234732" count="1">2002</citation>).

The above mentioned enzymatic components play a relevant role in mitigating heavy metal stress. <sentence_start/>Several studies have revealed that treatment of heavy metal enhances ROS formation, and thus, substantial increase in the activities of SOD, CAT, and APX was observed (Bharwana et al., <citation rid="B42" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4172/2155-6199.1000187" pmid="23911213" count="1">2013</citation>; Bashri and Prasad, <citation rid="B33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11738-014-1745-z" count="1">2015</citation>). <sentence_start/>A study by Wang et al. (<citation rid="B434" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2004</citation>) revealed a considerable increase in the activities of POD, APX, and SOD under Cu stress in <italic toggle="yes">B. juncea</italic> seedlings. <sentence_start/>Similarly, Bharwana et al. (<citation rid="B42" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4172/2155-6199.1000187" pmid="23911213" count="1">2013</citation>) showed that under Pb treatment, there was an appreciable rise in SOD, guaiacol peroxidase, APX and CAT activities, and their activities were further enhanced with the rising concentration of Pb from 50 to 100 μM. <sentence_start/>Similar to this, Singh et al. (<citation rid="B383" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.plaphy.2013.07.003" pmid="23917073" count="1">2013</citation>) reported increased activity of SOD and CAT under As exposure (5 and 50 μM). <sentence_start/>These results suggest that cooperative action of antioxidants is required for a detoxification mechanism under heavy metal stress.
“OMICS” tools
Metabolomics

Metabolomics refers to the identification and quantification of all low-molecular weight metabolites required by the organisms during developmental stages (Arbona et al., <citation rid="B16" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijms14034885" pmid="23455464" pmcid="PMC3634444" count="1">2013</citation>), and some metabolites have been reported to be involved under heavy metal stress tolerance strategies. <sentence_start/>In the following section, we discuss the role of metabolomics under heavy metal stress.
Amino acids and amines

Amino acids and their derivatives have been reported to chelate metal ions, thus conferring metal tolerance to plants. <sentence_start/>Amino acids, particularly proline and histidine, have been found to chelate metal ions in cells as well as in the xylem sap (Rai, <citation rid="B325" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1023/A:1022308229759" count="1">2002</citation>; Sharma and Dietz, <citation rid="B366" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jxb/erj073" pmid="16473893" count="1">2006</citation>). <sentence_start/>Proline has been reported to accumulate under heavy metal stress (Talanova et al., <citation rid="B399" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1023/A:1026735603890" count="1">2000</citation>; Yusuf et al., <citation rid="B468" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.plaphy.2012.05.004" pmid="22705589" count="1">2012a</citation>). <sentence_start/>A study on microalgae has demonstrated an increased level of proline under Cd stress (Siripornadulsil et al., <citation rid="B385" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1105/tpc.004853" pmid="12417705" pmcid="PMC152731" count="1">2002</citation>). <sentence_start/>The mechanism of action of increased levels of proline is not sequestration, but it reduces the formation of free radicals and also maintains reducing environment by enhancing the level of GSH (Siripornadulsil et al., <citation rid="B385" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1105/tpc.004853" pmid="12417705" pmcid="PMC152731" count="1">2002</citation>). <sentence_start/>Histidine, another important amino acid, has been found to play an important role under heavy metal stress. <sentence_start/>Krämer et al. (<citation rid="B215" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/379635a0" count="1">1996</citation>) reported increased histidine levels in the xylem sap of <italic toggle="yes">Alyssum lesbiacum</italic> (Ni hyperaccumulator) under Ni stress. <sentence_start/>Similarly, Kerkeb and Krämer (<citation rid="B198" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp102.010686" pmid="12586895" pmcid="PMC166847" count="1">2003</citation>) reported simultaneous uptake of Ni and Histidine in <italic toggle="yes">B. juncea</italic>. <sentence_start/>Changes in the histidine content have functional significance in metal stress tolerance (Sharma and Dietz, <citation rid="B366" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jxb/erj073" pmid="16473893" count="1">2006</citation>). <sentence_start/>NA (aminocarboxylate), an amino acid derivative synthesized by condensation process of three S-adenosyl-L-methionine, has been also reported to chelate metal ions. <sentence_start/>They have been found to be involved in the movement of mineral nutrients (Stephan and Scholz, <citation rid="B393" ref-type="bibr" count="1">1993</citation>). <sentence_start/>The physiological role of NA has been confirmed by studying the tomato mutant lacking NA synthase, an enzyme involved in catalyzing formation of NA, which showed accumulation of Fe and Cu (Scholz et al., <citation rid="B352" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1399-3054.1985.tb02825.x" count="1">1985</citation>; Herbik et al., <citation rid="B165" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.111.2.533" pmid="8787027" pmcid="PMC157864" count="1">1996</citation>). <sentence_start/>Apart from its chelating action, NA has been reported to be precursor of phytosiderophore mugineic acid involved in binding metals such as Zn, Cu, and Fe (Treeby et al., <citation rid="B410" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/BF02220801" count="1">1989</citation>).
Organic acids

Organic acids such as malate, citrate, and oxalate have been reported to transport metals through xylem and are involved in sequestrating ions in vacuole (Rauser, <citation rid="B329" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/BF02738153" pmid="10505666" count="1">1999</citation>). <sentence_start/>Citrate, synthesized from citrate synthase, has been shown to have high affinity for Fe, Ni, and Cd, but it is majorly involved in chelating Fe (Cataldo et al., <citation rid="B60" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.86.3.734" pmid="16665978" pmcid="PMC1054560" count="1">1988</citation>). <sentence_start/>Malate has been reported to chelate Zn and is mainly involved in chelating cytosolic ions (Mathys, <citation rid="B262" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1399-3054.1977.tb01509.x" count="1">1977</citation>).
Glutathione and α-tocopherol

Glutathione (GSH) is a water-soluble tripeptide thiol having low molecular weight (c-Glu-Cys-Gly) and plays a role in the cellular defense against the toxic actions of heavy metals (Meister and Anderson, <citation rid="B267" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1146/annurev.bi.52.070183.003431" pmid="6137189" count="1">1983</citation>). <sentence_start/>Glutathione reductase (GR) readily converts an oxidized glutathione (GSSG) form to reduced form of GSH. <sentence_start/>GR contains a conserved disulfide bridge that breaks off under metal stress (Creissen et al., <citation rid="B77" ref-type="bibr" pmid="1303792" count="1">1992</citation>; Lee et al., <citation rid="B232" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S0167-4781(97)00198-X" pmid="9512665" count="1">1998</citation>) and plays an important role in defense by reducing GSSG, thus allowing a high GSH/GSSG ratio to be maintained. <sentence_start/>Studies on <italic toggle="yes">Luffa</italic> seedlings showed an increasing trend in GR activity with an increasing concentration of As (Singh et al., <citation rid="B381" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00709-014-0753-6" pmid="25586108" count="1">2015</citation>). <sentence_start/>GR-catalyzed reduction of glutathione disulfide (GSSG) to glutathione (GSH) is NADPH dependent, and to maintain the proper ratio of GSH/GSSG, GSH biosynthesis must be initiated with rapid reduction in GSSG by GR (Kumar et al., <citation rid="B220" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.chemosphere.2012.05.070" pmid="22722003" count="1">2012</citation>).

Alpha-tocopherol is the most active form of vitamin E and is synthesized in the plastids of higher plants. <sentence_start/>It is found to be involved in scavenging ROS and lipid peroxides (Munne-Bosch, <citation rid="B289" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jplph.2005.04.022" pmid="16008098" count="1">2005</citation>) by quenching <sup>1</sup>O<sub>2</sub> in the chloroplast and thus, prevents cell membrane from damage under stress. <sentence_start/>Several studies have reported changes in the levels of α-tocopherol under heavy metal stress (Collin et al., <citation rid="B76" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1365-3040.2007.01755.x" pmid="17996014" count="1">2008</citation>; Yusuf et al., <citation rid="B467" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.bbabio.2010.02.002l" pmid="20144585" count="1">2010</citation>; Kumar et al., <citation rid="B220" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.chemosphere.2012.05.070" pmid="22722003" count="1">2012</citation>; Lushchak and Semchuk, <citation rid="B254" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11738-012-0988-9" count="1">2012</citation>). <sentence_start/>A study by Collin et al. (<citation rid="B76" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1365-3040.2007.01755.x" pmid="17996014" count="1">2008</citation>) reported an increased concentration of α-tocopherol in <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis</italic> under Cd treatment, and the authors suggested that there is an upregulation of genes related to its biosynthesis (Figure 3).
Phenols

Synthesis of phenolic compounds under heavy metal stress is due to their high tendency to chelate metals, which is due to the presence of hydroxyl and carboxyl groups that bind to metal ions particularly iron and copper (Jun et al., <citation rid="B193" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1365-2621.2003.tb07029.x" count="1">2003</citation>). <sentence_start/>Winkel-Shirley (<citation rid="B444" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S1369-5266(02)00256-X" pmid="11960739" count="1">2002</citation>) reported induction of phenolic compounds in maize under aluminum exposure. <sentence_start/>Similarly, Diáz et al. (<citation rid="B89" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S0168-9452(01)00410-1" count="1">2001</citation>) reported accumulation of phenols in leaves of <italic toggle="yes">P. vulgaris</italic> when exposed to Cu stress. <sentence_start/>This increase in phenolics is correlated with increased activity of enzymes involved in biosynthesis of phenols under heavy metal stress. <sentence_start/>Phenols have been reported to be directly involved in chelating Fe ions and thus, suppressing Fenton's reaction, which is the important source of ROS production. <sentence_start/>Stimulation of CHS (Chalcone synthase) and PAL (phenylalanine ammonia-lyase) activities has been reported in several plants exposed to Cu, Cd, Al, Pb, and Ni (Babu et al., <citation rid="B29" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/pcp/pcg160" pmid="14701927" count="1">2003</citation>; Sobkowiak and Deckert, <citation rid="B387" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jplph.2005.08.017" pmid="17032622" count="1">2006</citation>; Kováčik and Klejdus, <citation rid="B212" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00299-007-0490-9" pmid="18066553" count="1">2008</citation>; Kováčik et al., <citation rid="B213" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jplph.2009.03.002" pmid="19380176" count="1">2009</citation>; Pawlak-Sprada et al., <citation rid="B309" ref-type="bibr" pmid="21503278" count="1">2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>Lavid et al. (<citation rid="B228" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s004250000400" pmid="11289596" count="1">2001</citation>) reported that tea plants rich in tannin are tolerant to Mn and prevent from Mn toxicity by directly chelating the Mn.
Ionome and ionomics

Ionome includes the role of mineral nutrients, namely nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), potassium (K), calcium (Ca), sulfur (S) and magnesium (Mg) and trace metals namely iron (Fe), copper (Cu), manganese (Mn), molybdenum (Mo), cobalt (Co), and zinc (Zn) in alleviating heavy metal toxicity. <sentence_start/>Although all the mineral nutrients and trace elements are essential for growth and development processes of plants, concentration greater than the required level becomes toxic to the plants. <sentence_start/>Apart from posing toxicity at higher concentration, nutrients under safe limit play important role in alleviating toxicity induced by heavy metals.

Nitrogen is the most essential nutrient as it is the major constituent of proteins, nucleic acids, vitamins, and hormones. <sentence_start/>It has the potentiality of alleviating heavy metal toxicity, as it enhances the photosynthetic capacity by increasing chlorophyll synthesis, often synthesizes N-containing metabolites like proline, GSH, etc. and by enhancing the activity of antioxidant enzymes (Sharma and Dietz, <citation rid="B366" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jxb/erj073" pmid="16473893" count="1">2006</citation>; Lin et al., <citation rid="B243" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3923/brj.2011.13.19" count="1">2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>In a study by Pankovic et al. (<citation rid="B307" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1006/anbo.2000.1250" count="1">2000</citation>), it has been shown that supplementing 7.5 mM (optimal level) of N to sunflower reduced the inhibitory effect of Cd on photosynthesis by enhancing Rubisco activity and by increasing protein content. <sentence_start/>In another study by Zhu et al. (<citation rid="B484" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/01904167.2011.531363" count="1">2011</citation>), it has been shown that supplementing N fertilizer in the form of 16 mM (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, alleviated Cd-induced toxicity in <italic toggle="yes">Sedum</italic>. <sentence_start/>The alleviating potential not only depends on the supplemented level of N but also on the source of N. <sentence_start/>For instance, when N was applied in the form of -N, it reduced the Cd concentration in leaves of rice plants that was found to be below 100 mg kg<sup>−1</sup> (Jalloh et al., <citation rid="B186" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jhazmat.2008.05.146" pmid="18603363" count="1">2009</citation>), but when supplemented as N, it increased the Cd concentration, which suggests antagonistic behavior of - while synergistic of toward Cd. <sentence_start/>Another mineral nutrient, phosphorus (P) is the major constituent of cell membrane and nucleic acid, and majorly required for phosphorylation reaction. <sentence_start/>It has also been reported in alleviating metal-induced toxicity either by diluting the metal or by decreasing the mobility of the metal by forming metal-phosphate complex (Sarwar et al., <citation rid="B348" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/jsfa.3916" pmid="20355131" count="1">2010</citation>). <sentence_start/>In addition, P can also increase GSH content and prevent membrane damage, thereby conferring tolerance to plants (Wang et al., <citation rid="B432" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11099-009-0043-2" count="1">2009</citation>).

Potassium (K) ion is required by the plant to maintain anion-cation balance in cells and plays important regulatory role in protein synthesis and enzyme activation. <sentence_start/>By improving nutritional status of K, condition of oxidative stress in plants can be minimized (Shen et al., <citation rid="B368" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.124.1.431" pmid="10982456" pmcid="PMC59156" count="1">2000</citation>). <sentence_start/>Supplementation of K at 60 mg kg<sup>−1</sup> alleviated the toxicity induced by Cd at 25 mg kg<sup>−1</sup> by increasing the content of AsA and GSH. <sentence_start/>Similar to nitrogen, K source may also play an important role in alleviating toxicity. <sentence_start/>A study by Zhao et al. (<citation rid="B478" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S0160-4120(03)00081-3" pmid="14592574" count="1">2004</citation>) clearly demonstrated that application of KNO<sub>3</sub>, K<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, and KCl at the rate of 55, 110, and 166 mg.<sentence_start/>K.kg<sup>−1</sup>, respectively, to the soil has differential effect on Cd (concentration 15 mg Kg<sup>−1</sup>) accumulation. <sentence_start/>When KCl and K<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> were applied in increasing concentration from 0 to 55 mg kg<sup>−1</sup>, there was 60-90% increase in Cd accumulation in shoots, whereas similar increasing concentrations of KNO<sub>3</sub> increased the Cd content very marginally, suggesting its protective action against Cd stress.

Sulfur (S), another mineral nutrient, serves as an important constituent of several coenzymes, vitamins, and ferredoxin. <sentence_start/>Wangeline et al.
