(<citation rid="B436" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2134/jeq2004.5400" pmid="14964358" count="1">2004</citation>) reported that Cd toxicity could be alleviated by the upregulation of S-assimilation pathway, thus suggesting toward alleviating role of S under heavy metal toxicity. <sentence_start/>Studies on <italic toggle="yes">Triticum aestivum</italic> (Khan et al., <citation rid="B202" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1439-037X.2007.00272.x" count="1">2007</citation>), <italic toggle="yes">B. juncea</italic> (Wangeline et al., <citation rid="B436" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2134/jeq2004.5400" pmid="14964358" count="1">2004</citation>), and <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis</italic> (Howarth et al., <citation rid="B177" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1023/A:1022349623951" pmid="12650624" count="1">2003</citation>) have shown increased ATP-sulfurylase (ATPS) and serine acetyl transferase (SAT) activities under Cd stress, and thereby conferring tolerance to these plants. <sentence_start/>As ATPS activity helps in maintaining GSH level required for regulating Ascorbate (AsA)-GSH cycle (Khan et al., <citation rid="B201" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1134/S1021443709050136" count="1">2009</citation>), it has been reported that S at 40 mg.<sentence_start/>S.Kg<sup>−1</sup> enhanced the AsA-GSH cycle, thereby reducing Cd-induced toxicity in mustard (Anjum et al., <citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10725-007-9251-6" count="1">2008</citation>). <sentence_start/>Thus, indicating toward the possibility that S supplementation to soil system might enhance the formation of S-containing defense compounds such as GSH and phytochelatins. <sentence_start/>Study by Astolfi et al. (<citation rid="B24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jplph.2003.11.005" pmid="15310068" count="1">2004</citation>) has shown that Cd (100 μM) exposure enhanced the ATPS, <italic toggle="yes">O</italic>-acetyl serine (OAS) thiol lyase activity, which is related to the production of phytochelatins that play the most effective detoxifying mechanism in plants (Zhang et al., <citation rid="B476" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1365-3040.2010.02144.x" pmid="20233337" count="1">2010</citation>). <sentence_start/>Apart from enhancing the formation of phytochelatins, S also regulates ethylene signaling and thereby helping under heavy metal stress (Masood et al., <citation rid="B261" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1365-3040.2011.02432.x" pmid="21950968" count="1">2012</citation>). <sentence_start/>Calcium (Ca) is majorly involved in activating the enzymes and also plays an important role in regulating metabolic activities. <sentence_start/>Due to chemical similarity as well as due to same channels and intracellular Ca-binding sites (Lauer Júnior et al., <citation rid="B227" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1574-6968.2008.01214.x" pmid="18510555" count="1">2008</citation>) of Ca<sup>+2</sup> and Cd<sup>+2</sup>, Cd present in external medium, replaces the Ca, and thereby affects the growth of plant. <sentence_start/>However, Ca has been shown to decrease the heavy metal-induced toxicity (Suzuki, <citation rid="B397" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5511/plantbiotechnology.22.19" count="1">2005</citation>; Farzadfar et al., <citation rid="B111" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11356-012-1181-9" pmid="22968674" count="1">2013</citation>). <sentence_start/>It has been reported that 30 mM Ca reduced the Cd content from 46.7 to 17.4 μg in <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis</italic> seedlings (Suzuki, <citation rid="B397" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5511/plantbiotechnology.22.19" count="1">2005</citation>). <sentence_start/>Similar to this, Zhenyan et al. (<citation rid="B480" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.plantsci.2004.07.001" count="1">2005</citation>) reported enhanced Cd (concentration 0.5 mM) tolerance in <italic toggle="yes">Lactuca sativa</italic> when supplied with 4 mM CaCl<sub>2</sub>, which was due to enhanced expression of phytochelatin synthase. <sentence_start/>Ca reduces heavy metal-induced toxicity by reducing their uptake, influencing physiological processes, or activating expressions of other defense compounds.

Magnesium (Mg), an important constituent for chlorophyll biosynthesis, plays an essential role under heavy metal toxicity. <sentence_start/>Abul Kashem and Kawai (<citation rid="B1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1747-0765.2007.00129.x" count="1">2007</citation>) reported that Cd (0.25 μM) -induced toxicity in Japanese mustard spinach was alleviated by Mg at 10 mM, and Cd accumulation was reduced by 40%. <sentence_start/>Mg-induced alleviation is not due to inhibition in uptake but due to enhanced antioxidant enzymes (Chou et al., <citation rid="B71" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jplph.2010.12.004" pmid="21216027" count="1">2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>Moreover, Mg-induced alleviation has been also correlated with expression of some genes <italic toggle="yes">OsIRT</italic>1, <italic toggle="yes">OsZIP</italic>1, and <italic toggle="yes">OsZIP</italic>3 of rice.

Trace elements are required in lesser amount for the biological system, which include iron (Fe), copper (Cu), manganese (Mn), molybdenum (Mo), cobalt (Co), and zinc (Zn), and their high levels could be toxic. <sentence_start/>The essentialities of these trace metals are due to their active participation in the redox reactions as well as because of their roles as enzyme cofactors (Sanita di Toppi and Gabbrielli, <citation rid="B345" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S0098-8472(98)00058-6" count="1">1999</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, apart from their roles in biological system, they have been reported to play a crucial role in alleviating metal toxicity. <sentence_start/>Several trace elements have direct as well as indirect effects on heavy metal availability and toxicity (Sarwar et al., <citation rid="B348" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/jsfa.3916" pmid="20355131" count="1">2010</citation>). <sentence_start/>Direct effects include lowered solubility of heavy metals in the soil (Hart et al., <citation rid="B157" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8137.2005.01416.x" pmid="15998393" count="1">2005</citation>; Shi et al., <citation rid="B370" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11104-004-3920-2" count="1">2005</citation>; Matusik et al., <citation rid="B264" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jhazmat.2007.08.010" pmid="17868991" count="1">2008</citation>), competition between heavy metals and trace elements for the same membrane transporters (Baszynski et al., <citation rid="B36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1399-3054.1980.tb03269.x" count="1">1980</citation>; Qiu et al., <citation rid="B323" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/BF02856167" count="1">2005</citation>), and heavy metal sequestration in the vacuoles (Salt and Rauser, <citation rid="B340" ref-type="bibr" pmid="12228436" doi="10.1104/pp.107.4.1293" pmcid="PMC157264" count="1">1995</citation>; Zaccheo et al., <citation rid="B470" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11104-005-4791-x" count="1">2006</citation>). <sentence_start/>Indirect effects include dilution of heavy metal concentration by increasing plant biomass (dilution effect) and alleviation of heavy metal stress by increasing antioxidant defense system (Hassan et al., <citation rid="B158" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/jpln.200420403" count="1">2005</citation>; Suzuki, <citation rid="B397" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5511/plantbiotechnology.22.19" count="1">2005</citation>; Jalloh et al., <citation rid="B186" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jhazmat.2008.05.146" pmid="18603363" count="1">2009</citation>). <sentence_start/>Zn, being an important group of metal transporter family, has been suggested to prevent damage caused by Cd toxicity. <sentence_start/>As reported in the case of <italic toggle="yes">Thalpsi violacea</italic>, plants supplied with 2 mgL<sup>−1</sup> Cd showed 48.5 mg Kg<sup>−1</sup> Zn accumulation than that of control (16.8 mgKg<sup>−1</sup>), whereas when the plant was supplemented with 5 mgL<sup>−1</sup> Cd, Zn accumulation decreased upto 12.8 mg Kg<sup>−1</sup>, suggesting Cd/Zn antagonism (Street et al., <citation rid="B394" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.sajb.2009.12.006" count="1">2010</citation>). <sentence_start/>Furthermore, Zn also enhances the activities of antioxidant enzymes and competes with Cd to bind with the membrane protein in order to protect plant (Wu and Zhang, <citation rid="B447" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1081/PLN-120004380" count="1">2002</citation>). <sentence_start/>Other trace metal Fe, under Cd stress, showed reduced Cd uptake and translocation, thus increasing plant growth. <sentence_start/>Study by Qureshi et al. (<citation rid="B324" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jplph.2010.01.017" pmid="20199821" count="1">2010</citation>) revealed that exogenous application of 40 μM Fe reduces the condition of oxidative stress by stabilizing the thylakoid complex under Cd stress. <sentence_start/>It was also reported that at Fe concentrations of 1.89 mg L<sup>−1</sup> (moderate) and 16.8 mg L<sup>−1</sup> (high), under low level of Cd (0.1 mM), plant height showed increment (Nada et al., <citation rid="B292" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11738-006-0009-y" count="1">2007</citation>).

Similarly, studies have also revealed the protective roles of trace elements in ameliorating toxic effects of heavy metals by protecting photosynthetic tissue and increasing antioxidant capacity (Zornoza et al., <citation rid="B488" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jplph.2010.02.011" pmid="20399531" count="1">2010</citation>; Tkalec et al., <citation rid="B407" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0087582" pmid="24475312" pmcid="PMC3903775" count="1">2014</citation>). <sentence_start/>Pa1'ove-Balang et al. (<citation rid="B305" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2006</citation>) have shown that Mn-mediated amelioration of Cd toxicity was associated with a decreased Cd uptake. <sentence_start/>Apart from the beneficial role played by trace metals, there are some beneficial nutrients like selenium (Se), and silicon (Si) that also play a major role under heavy metal stress. <sentence_start/>Earlier, selenium (Se) was considered as toxic element but later on Schwarz and Foltz (<citation rid="B354" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/ja01569a087" pmid="10408880" count="1">1957</citation>) confirmed it to be an essential one. <sentence_start/>Studies on lettuce grown under Pb and Cd toxicity supplemented with Se showed a decrease in heavy metal accumulation as well as enhanced uptake of essential nutrients (He et al., <citation rid="B163" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S0160-4120(03)00167-3" pmid="14749105" count="1">2004</citation>). <sentence_start/>Belokobylsky et al. (<citation rid="B39" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1023/B:JRNC.0000015807.53132.c0" count="1">2004</citation>) and Feng and Wei (<citation rid="B112" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2012</citation>) have found that Se level up to 5 mg L<sup>−1</sup> has beneficial effects on <italic toggle="yes">Spirulina platensis</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">P. vittata</italic>, respectively. <sentence_start/>Filek et al. (<citation rid="B116" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jplph.2007.06.006" pmid="17913288" count="1">2008</citation>) have shown that exogenous application of Se alleviates toxic effects of Cd by enhancing the activities of antioxidant enzymes such as SOD, CAT, GPX, and APX. <sentence_start/>Several reports have revealed that appropriate dose of Se can protect plants against damage by heavy metals such as Hg, Pb, Cd, Cr, and Sb (Khattak et al., <citation rid="B203" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2134/jeq1991.00472425002000010026x" count="1">1991</citation>; Shanker et al., <citation rid="B359" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/BF00011438" count="1">1996</citation>; Belokobylsky et al., <citation rid="B39" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1023/B:JRNC.0000015807.53132.c0" count="1">2004</citation>; He et al., <citation rid="B163" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S0160-4120(03)00167-3" pmid="14749105" count="1">2004</citation>; Feng et al., <citation rid="B113" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.microc.2010.06.003" count="1">2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>Role of Si under heavy metal stress is also well established (Singh et al., <citation rid="B384" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s12011-011-9118-6" pmid="21681465" count="1">2011b</citation>; Dragišić Maksimović et al., <citation rid="B96" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jxb/err359" pmid="22249995" count="1">2012</citation>; Tripathi et al., <citation rid="B411" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11738-011-0826-5" count="1">2012</citation>). <sentence_start/>Study by Song et al. (<citation rid="B388" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jhazmat.2009.06.143" pmid="19616891" count="1">2009</citation>) has shown that supplementation of Si under Cd stress decreased an uptake and root to shoot translocation of Cd as well as enhanced the activities of enzymes of the defense machinery in <italic toggle="yes">B. chinensis</italic>. <sentence_start/>Similarly, study by Bharwana et al. (<citation rid="B42" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4172/2155-6199.1000187" pmid="23911213" count="1">2013</citation>) revealed that Si application reduces Pb uptake and enhances the activities of antioxidants <italic toggle="yes">viz</italic>., SOD, GPX, APX, and CAT.

The measurement of elemental composition and their changes as a response to some stimuli in living organisms comes under the study of ionomics. <sentence_start/>Alteration in ionome could be direct or indirect. <sentence_start/>Direct one includes the changes in nutrient level in soil or due to impairment of ion transporter, whereas indirect changes might be due to changes in cell wall structure (Salt et al., <citation rid="B341" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1146/annurev.arplant.59.032607.092942" pmid="18251712" count="1">2008</citation>). <sentence_start/>Heavy metals due to their interaction with nutrient elements affect the uptake and distribution of these elements and may result in deficiency of minerals thus affecting the growth. <sentence_start/>Sarwar et al. (<citation rid="B348" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/jsfa.3916" pmid="20355131" count="1">2010</citation>) suggested that Cd affects the permeability of plasma membrane and thus interferes with the nutrient uptake. <sentence_start/>However, there exists both antagonistic as well as synergistic interaction between heavy metals and micronutrient uptake, which could be due to differences in plant species and nutrient concentration. <sentence_start/>Likewise, a study by Cataldo et al. (<citation rid="B59" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.73.3.844" pmid="16663310" pmcid="PMC1066558" count="1">1983</citation>) reported antagonistic interaction between Cd and Fe, Zn, Cu, and Mn in soybean plants, whereas Nan et al. (<citation rid="B298" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S0048-9697(01)00919-6" pmid="11874041" count="1">2002</citation>) reported synergistic interaction between Cd and Zn in wheat and corn. <sentence_start/>In a study by Yang et al. (<citation rid="B457" ref-type="bibr" count="1">1998</citation>), decreased accumulation of Fe, Mn, and Cu in ryegrass, maize, cabbage, and white clover was observed after Cd exposure, whereas there was increased P accumulation. <sentence_start/>Similarly, Cui et al. (<citation rid="B78" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S1001-0742(08)60052-2" pmid="18595401" count="1">2008</citation>) reported decrease in Fe and Zn uptake in rice after Cd treatment in hydroponic system. <sentence_start/>A study by Safarzadeh et al. (<citation rid="B338" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/03650340.2011.622752" count="1">2013</citation>) determined the effect of different doses (0, 45, and 90 mg kg soil) of Cd on uptake of Fe, Zn, Cu, and Mn in seven rice cultivar and reported decrease in Zn, Fe, Mn, and Cu uptake. <sentence_start/>Not only the uptake decreased but also there was decrease in the translocation of these minerals as Cu and Fe contents found to be greater in roots than in shoots that indicate toward impairment of ions transporters.

Similar to Cd, As has also been reported to influence nutrient uptake and their distribution in plants. <sentence_start/>Meharg and Hartley-Whitaker (<citation rid="B266" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1046/j.1469-8137.2002.00363.x" count="1">2002</citation>) reported As-induced decrease in P uptake is due to chemical similarity between P and arsenate and due to which arsenate enters the plant via the phosphate transport systems. <sentence_start/>However, the concentration of As also plays an important role in P uptake. <sentence_start/>Burló et al. (<citation rid="B50" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/jf9806560" pmid="10552445" count="1">1999</citation>) reported higher uptake of P at lower level of As in tomato plants. <sentence_start/>Similarly, Carbonell et al. (<citation rid="B55" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S0048-9697(98)00195-8" count="1">1998</citation>) reported increased P uptake in tomato plant when exposed to low level of As. <sentence_start/>As not only influences P uptake but also affects the uptake of other nutrients like N, P, K, Ca, etc. <sentence_start/>A study by Carbonell-Barrachina et al. (<citation rid="B56" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/01904169709365361" count="1">1997</citation>) observed increased concentration of N, P, K, Ca, and Mg in <italic toggle="yes">P. vulgaris</italic> L. plants when exposed to arsenite. <sentence_start/>Similarly, Carbonell-Barrachina et al. (<citation rid="B57" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/01904169409364853" count="1">1994</citation>) reported decreased uptake of K, Ca, and Mg (macronutrinets), B, Cu, Mn, and Zn (micronutrinets) in <italic toggle="yes">Lycopersicum esculentum</italic> Mill. <sentence_start/>The effect of As concentration on nutrient level of hyperaccumulator <italic toggle="yes">P. vittata</italic> L. had also been studied by Tu and Ma (<citation rid="B414" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.envpol.2004.03.026" pmid="15734593" count="1">2005</citation>), and the authors reported that both micro- and macronutrients were in the range of normal concentration as in non-hyperaccumulators. <sentence_start/>However, there was enhancement in P and K contents in the fronds of <italic toggle="yes">P. vittata</italic> L. at lower level of As. <sentence_start/>They reported molar ratio of P/As to be 1.0 in fronds of <italic toggle="yes">P. vittata</italic> L., which is the threshold value for normal growth of plants.

Heavy metal ions such as Cu<sup>+2</sup>, Zn<sup>+2</sup>, Mn<sup>+2</sup>, and Fe<sup>+2</sup> are essential for plant metabolism but when they are present in excess amount become highly toxic. <sentence_start/>For instance, Zn and Mn when present in excess impairs growth and compete with Fe. <sentence_start/>Excess Fe in the plant system participates in the fenton reaction, thereby creating a condition of oxidative stress (Williams and Pittman, <citation rid="B442" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2010</citation>; Shanmugam et al., <citation rid="B360" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8137.2010.03606.x" pmid="21219335" count="1">2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>In order to avoid toxicity induced by mineral elements and trace elements, these are chelated by low molecular weight compounds and sequestrated in vacuoles or excluded to extracellular spaces by transporters situated in the tonoplast or plasma membrane, which plays central role in maintaining metal homeostasis under safe limit. <sentence_start/>These transporters belong to (1) P<sub>1B</sub>-ATPase or CPx-type ATPase, (2) Cation Diffusion Facilitator (CDF) also known as Metal Tolerance Proteins (MTPs), (3) Natural Resistance-Associated Macrophage Proteins (NRAMPs), and (4) ZRT-IRT-like Protein (ZIP) transporters.
P<sub>1B</sub>-ATPases (also known as heavy metal ATPases: HMAs)

P<sub>1B</sub>-ATPases (also known as Heavy Metal ATPases: <italic toggle="yes">HMAs</italic>) are found in a wide range of organisms ranging from prokaryotes to eukaryotes including yeasts, insect, mammals, and plants. <sentence_start/>Being energized by ATP hydrolysis, they translocate heavy metals (Zn, Co, Cu, Cd, and Pb) out of cytoplasm (to plasma membrane and into vacuole) and thus play important roles in their transport, compartmentalization, and detoxification (Williams et al., <citation rid="B443" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S0005-2736(00)00133-4" pmid="10748249" count="1">2000</citation>; Grennan, <citation rid="B141" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.109.900287" pmid="19339509" pmcid="PMC2663745" count="1">2009</citation>). <sentence_start/>HMA members (HMA2, HMA3, and HMA4) export Zn and Cd. <sentence_start/>For instance, HMA4 protein that plays a role in nutrition and transport of Zn from root to shoot also protects plants from Cd <italic toggle="yes">via</italic> its efflux (Mills et al., <citation rid="B274" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.febslet.2004.12.040" pmid="15670847" count="1">2005</citation>). <sentence_start/>Hussain et al. (<citation rid="B179" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1105/tpc.020487" pmid="15100400" pmcid="PMC423219" count="1">2004</citation>) demonstrated that though HMA2 and HMA4 are essential for Zn homeostasis in <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis</italic>, double mutants of HMA2 and HMA4 (<italic toggle="yes">hma2</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">hma4</italic>) exhibited increased sensitivity of plant to Cd, suggesting that they may also play a role in Cd detoxification. <sentence_start/>Similarly, loss of function in HMA2 and HMA4 has been shown to increase Cd sensitivity in <italic toggle="yes">Arabidops</italic>is under phytochelatins deficient, <italic toggle="yes">cad1-3</italic> as well as CAD1 backgrounds (Wong and Cobbett, <citation rid="B445" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8137.2008.02638.x" pmid="19076718" count="1">2009</citation>). <sentence_start/>A recent study on 349 wild varieties of <italic toggle="yes">A. thaliana</italic> with combined approach of genome-wide association mapping, linkage mapping, and transgenic complementation revealed that HMA3 is solely responsible for variation in amount of Cd accumulated. <sentence_start/>Varieties with high Cd accumulation indicate toward reduced HMA3 function (Chao et al., <citation rid="B63" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pgen.1002923" pmid="22969436" pmcid="PMC3435251" count="1">2012</citation>). <sentence_start/>Similarly, Song et al. (<citation rid="B389" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.1414968111" pmid="25331872" pmcid="PMC4226097" count="1">2014</citation>) found expression of C-type ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter (OsABCC) family in <italic toggle="yes">Oryza sativa</italic> and reported its involvement in detoxifying and reducing As accumulation in grains. <sentence_start/>They reported higher expression of these transporters under higher level of As.
Cation diffusion facilitators (CDFs) or metal tolerance proteins (MTPs)

Cation Diffusion Facilitators (CDFs), also known as Metal Tolerance Proteins (MTPs) family, were first reported by Nies and Silver (<citation rid="B301" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/BF01569902" pmid="7766211" count="1">1995</citation>) and found in diverse group of organisms such as bacteria, fungi, animals, and plants. <sentence_start/>Members of this family are involved in cellular heavy metals homeostasis with principal selectivity for Zn<sup>2+</sup>, Mn<sup>2+</sup>, and Fe<sup>2+</sup> (Podar et al., <citation rid="B318" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1074/jbc.m111.305649" pmid="22139846" pmcid="PMC3270973" count="1">2012</citation>). <sentence_start/>Despite their specificities for Zn<sup>2+</sup>, Mn<sup>2+</sup>, and Fe<sup>2+</sup>, many CDFs may also transport other heavy metals such as Co<sup>2+</sup>, Ni<sup>2+</sup>, and Cd<sup>2+</sup> (Ricachenevsky et al., <citation rid="B332" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fpls.2013.00144" pmid="23717323" pmcid="PMC3653063" count="1">2013</citation>). <sentence_start/>CDFs transporters are involved in heavy metals efflux from the cytoplasm either to the extracellular space or into the organelles (Haney et al., <citation rid="B154" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10295-005-0224-3" pmid="15889311" count="1">2005</citation>; Peiter et al., <citation rid="B310" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.0609507104" pmid="17494768" pmcid="PMC1895984" count="1">2007</citation>; Ricachenevsky et al., <citation rid="B332" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fpls.2013.00144" pmid="23717323" pmcid="PMC3653063" count="1">2013</citation>). <sentence_start/>Twelve <italic toggle="yes">MTP</italic> genes have been recognized so far in <italic toggle="yes">A. thaliana</italic> and 10 in <italic toggle="yes">O. sativa</italic> (Gustin et al., <citation rid="B146" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/1471-2148-11-76" pmid="21435223" pmcid="PMC3073911" count="1">2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>In <italic toggle="yes">A. thaliana</italic>, the first <italic toggle="yes">CDF</italic> gene was characterized as the <italic toggle="yes">Zinc Transporter 1</italic> gene (<italic toggle="yes">ZAT1</italic>) and later renamed as <italic toggle="yes">METAL TOLERANCE PROTEIN 1 (AtMTP1)</italic> (van der Zaal et al., <citation rid="B419" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.119.3.1047" pmid="10069843" pmcid="PMC32086" count="1">1999</citation>; Delhaize et al., <citation rid="B87" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1105/tpc.009134" pmid="12724539" pmcid="PMC153721" count="1">2003</citation>). <sentence_start/>The <italic toggle="yes">AtMTP1</italic> gene is expressed constitutively in roots as well as in shoots, and when overexpressed in <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis</italic>, it enhances Zn tolerance (van der Zaal et al., <citation rid="B419" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.119.3.1047" pmid="10069843" pmcid="PMC32086" count="1">1999</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, RNA interference (RNAi)-mediated silencing (Desbrosses-Fonrouge et al., <citation rid="B88" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.febslet.2005.06.046" pmid="16038907" count="1">2005</citation>) or T-DNA insertion mutation (Kobae et al., <citation rid="B209" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/pcp/pci015" pmid="15653794" count="1">2004</citation>) of this gene increases Zn sensitivity, indicating its important role in regulation of Zn homeostasis. <sentence_start/>In <italic toggle="yes">A. halleri</italic>, a Zn hyperaccumulator plant, <italic toggle="yes">AhMTP1</italic> gene is believed to have a role in Zn hypertolerance (Shahzad et al., <citation rid="B357" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pgen.1000911" pmid="20419142" pmcid="PMC2855318" count="1">2010</citation>). <sentence_start/>Unlike <italic toggle="yes">AtMTP1</italic> gene, <italic toggle="yes">AtMTP3</italic> is expressed predominantly in roots and reported to be engaged in maintenance of Zn homeostasis by excluding Zn under Zn oversupply (Arrivault et al., <citation rid="B18" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1365-313X.2006.02746.x" pmid="16709200" count="1">2006</citation>). <sentence_start/>Another member of MTPs family, <italic toggle="yes">AtMTP11</italic>, has been reported to transport as well as provide Mn tolerance (Delhaize et al., <citation rid="B86" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1365-313X.2007.03138.x" pmid="17559518" count="1">2007</citation>; Peiter et al., <citation rid="B310" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.0609507104" pmid="17494768" pmcid="PMC1895984" count="1">2007</citation>). <sentence_start/>In rice, an ortholog of MTPs, <italic toggle="yes">OsMTP1</italic>, has been characterized and supposed to be located on chromosome 5 and highly expressed in mature leaves and stem (Lan et al., <citation rid="B223" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11033-012-2162-2" pmid="23070916" count="1">2012</citation>; Yuan et al., <citation rid="B464" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.plaphy.2012.09.004" pmid="23031845" count="1">2012</citation>).

Menguer et al. (<citation rid="B269" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jxb/ert136" pmid="23761487" pmcid="PMC3697945" count="1">2013</citation>) demonstrated that <italic toggle="yes">OsMTP1</italic> gene localized on tonoplast, and when heterologously expressed in the yeast-mutant <italic toggle="yes">zrc1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">cot1</italic>, complemented Zn hypersensitivity. <sentence_start/>Besides, its expression also alleviated Co sensitivity, rescued Fe hypersensitivity of the <italic toggle="yes">ccc1</italic> mutant, and restored growth of the Cd-hypersensitive mutant <italic toggle="yes">ycf1</italic>, indicating potential role of this gene in possible biotechnological applications, such as bio fortification and phytoremediation.
Natural resistance-associated macrophage proteins (NRAMPs) transporters

Nramp is a highly conserved family of integral membrane proteins that are conserved in different species and located in the plasma membrane of root apical cells (Simões et al., <citation rid="B377" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4238/2012.July.19.14" pmid="22869550" count="1">2012</citation>). <sentence_start/>They are involved in proton-coupled active transport of various heavy metals(Fe<sup>2+</sup>, Zn<sup>2+</sup>, Mn<sup>2+</sup>, Co<sup>2+</sup>, Cd<sup>2+</sup>, Cu<sup>2+</sup>, Ni<sup>2+</sup>, and Pb<sup>2+</sup>) in wide range of organisms including bacteria, fungi, animals, and plants (Hall and Williams, <citation rid="B150" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jxb/erg303" pmid="14585824" count="1">2003</citation>; Cailliatte et al., <citation rid="B52" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1042/BJ20090655" pmid="19545236" count="1">2009</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, the physiological role of NRAMP was primarily related with Fe and to a lesser extent for Mn transport (Cailliatte et al., <citation rid="B52" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1042/BJ20090655" pmid="19545236" count="1">2009</citation>). <sentence_start/>AtNRAMP1 and 6, forms the first group, and AtNRAMP2-5 constitute the second group (Mäser et al., <citation rid="B260" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.126.4.1646" pmid="11500563" pmcid="PMC117164" count="1">2001</citation>). <sentence_start/>Of these, <italic toggle="yes">AtNRAMP1, 3, 4</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">6</italic> have been shown to encode functional plant heavy metal transporters (Krämer et al., <citation rid="B217" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.febslet.2007.04.010" pmid="17462635" count="1">2007</citation>; Cailliatte et al., <citation rid="B52" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1042/BJ20090655" pmid="19545236" count="1">2009</citation>). <sentence_start/>Yeast mutants defective in heavy metals uptake have been utilized to investigate transport specificities of plant Nramps. <sentence_start/>Study revealed that <italic toggle="yes">AtNRAMP1</italic> can complement the <italic toggle="yes">fet3fet4</italic> yeast mutant that is defective in both low and high-affinity Fe transporters, whereas overexpression of <italic toggle="yes">AtNRAMP1</italic> in <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis</italic> increases plant resistance to toxic Fe concentrations (Curie et al., <citation rid="B81" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1042/bj3470749" pmid="10769179" pmcid="PMC1221012" count="1">2000</citation>). <sentence_start/>Furthermore, AtNRAMP3 and AtNRAMP4 have been shown to mediate the remobilization of Fe from the vacuolar store and are essential for seed germination under low Fe conditions (Thomine et al., <citation rid="B403" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1046/j.1365-313X.2003.01760.x" pmid="12787249" count="1">2003</citation>; Lanquar et al., <citation rid="B226" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/sj.emboj.7600864" pmid="16270029" pmcid="PMC1356305" count="1">2005</citation>), indicating a role of Nramps in Fe homeostasis.

Since the roles of NRAMPs family proteins were previously related with Fe uptake and transport in biological systems, however, increasing numbers of studies indicated that members of this family have wide range of specificities for pumping cations inside and/or outside the cell. <sentence_start/>Cailliatte et al. (<citation rid="B53" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1105/tpc.109.073023" pmid="20228245" pmcid="PMC2861449" count="1">2010</citation>) demonstrated that NRAMP1, localized on plasma membrane, restores the capacity of the <italic toggle="yes">iron-regulated transporter1</italic> (a ZIP family metal transporter) mutant to take up Fe and Co, indicating that NRAMP1 has a broad selectivity for heavy metals <italic toggle="yes">in-vivo</italic>. <sentence_start/>An <italic toggle="yes">AtNRAMP4</italic> homolog, <italic toggle="yes">TjNRAMP4</italic>, was cloned from the Ni hyperaccumulator <italic toggle="yes">Thlaspi japonicum</italic>, and its expression increased Ni<sup>2+</sup> sensitivity of wild-type yeast due to elevated Ni accumulation, indicating that this protein might transport Ni into the cytoplasm (Mizuno et al., <citation rid="B282" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.plaphy.2005.07.006" pmid="16198592" count="1">2005</citation>). <sentence_start/>Besides regulating uptake and distribution of essential heavy metals, Nramps have also been found to be involved in the transport of non-essential heavy metals. <sentence_start/>In <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis, AtNRAMP3</italic> disruption increases Cd<sup>2+</sup> resistance, whereas overexpression of this gene confers increased Cd<sup>2+</sup> sensitivity, indicating that it plays a role in Cd<sup>2+</sup> transport and sensitivity in plant (Thomine et al., <citation rid="B404" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.97.9.4991" pmcid="PMC18345" pmid="10781110" count="1">2000</citation>; Mäser et al., <citation rid="B260" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.126.4.1646" pmid="11500563" pmcid="PMC117164" count="1">2001</citation>).

A <italic toggle="yes">O. sativa</italic> Nrat1 (<italic toggle="yes">OsNrat1</italic>) gene, a Nramp aluminum transporter and localized at all cells of root tips, when expressed in yeast transports only Al<sup>3+</sup> but not the Mn, Fe, and Cd, indicating that this transporter gene specifically transports only Al (Xia et al., <citation rid="B450" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8137.2011.03745.x" pmid="21564100" count="1">2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>Furthermore, in knockout of Nrat1, Al sensitivity increased, whereas in wild type, its expression is up-regulated by Al in root that is believed to be required for a prior step of final Al detoxification through sequestration of Al into vacuoles. <sentence_start/>Study of Cailliatte et al. (<citation rid="B52" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1042/BJ20090655" pmid="19545236" count="1">2009</citation>) demonstrated that <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis</italic> transgenic plants overexpressing <italic toggle="yes">AtNRAMP6</italic> gene were hypersensitive to Cd, although plant Cd content remained unchanged, thereby indicating that modification in expression pattern of <italic toggle="yes">AtNRAMP6</italic> affects distribution and availability of Cd within the cell. <sentence_start/>However, Sano et al. (<citation rid="B346" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2012</citation>) have shown that <italic toggle="yes">Nicotiana tabacum</italic> NRAMP1 gene (<italic toggle="yes">NtNRAMP1</italic>), a plasma membrane transporter, when overexpressed in tobacco BY-2 cells increases resistance of the cells to both Fe and Cd, and suggested that <italic toggle="yes">NtNRAMP1</italic> moderates Fe-uptake and prevents toxicity resulting from excess Fe or Cd application. <sentence_start/>Tiwari et al. (<citation rid="B406" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/pce.12138" pmid="23700971" count="1">2014</citation>) also demonstrated that <italic toggle="yes">OsNRAPM1</italic>, localized on plasma membrane of endodermis and pericycle cell, when expressed in <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis</italic> provides tolerance against As and Cd with their enhanced accumulation in root and shoot, and proposed that modification in this gene may be helpful in reducing the risk of food chain contamination by these toxic heavy metals. <sentence_start/>These studies clearly indicate that NRAMP genes are able to encode multi-specific heavy metals transporters. <sentence_start/>In recent years, a new Nramp5 belonging to rice (<italic toggle="yes">Os</italic> Nramp5) has been characterized, which is responsible for accumulation of Mn in rice and has been reported to encode proteins localized on plasma membrane, thus suggesting that Nramp5 is a major transporter responsible for transport of Mn and Cd (Sasaki et al., <citation rid="B349" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1105/tpc.112.096925" pmid="22589467" pmcid="PMC3442593" count="1">2012</citation>). <sentence_start/>To gain deep insights into the roles of <italic toggle="yes">NRAMP</italic> genes transporter in heavy metals uptake and homeostasis in plants, a more systematic characterization of the different members of the NRAMP family is further required.
ZRT, IRT-like proteins (ZIP) transporters

Members of the ZIP family named on the first member identified ZRT IRT- like Protein in Arabidopsis, expressed in roots of iron deficient plants and found to be capable of transporting various heavy metals such as Fe, Zn, Mn, Cd and Ni within cellular systems (Mäser et al., <citation rid="B260" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.126.4.1646" pmid="11500563" pmcid="PMC117164" count="1">2001</citation>). <sentence_start/>The key feature of the ZIP family is that these proteins can transport heavy metals from the extracellular space or from organelles lumen into the cytoplasm. <sentence_start/>In <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis</italic>, 15 genes <italic toggle="yes">viz. ZIP1-12, IRT1, IRT2</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">IRT3</italic> of the ZIP family are reported (Milner et al., <citation rid="B276" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jxb/ers315" pmid="23264639" pmcid="PMC3528025" count="1">2013</citation>). <sentence_start/>Among these members, AtIRT1, AtIRT2, and AtIRT3 transporters are well characterized, with AtIRT1 being the most studied (Eide et al., <citation rid="B99" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.93.11.5624" pmid="8643627" pmcid="PMC39298" count="1">1996</citation>; Lin et al., <citation rid="B244" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8137.2009.02766.x" pmid="19210716" count="1">2009</citation>; Vert et al., <citation rid="B424" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00425-009-0904-8" pmid="19252923" count="1">2009</citation>) for their involvement in regulation of Zn and Fe homeostasis in plants. <sentence_start/>Rest of the ZIP family members has been studied for their membrane localization and heavy metals they transport into or outside of a specific organelle (Milner et al., <citation rid="B276" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jxb/ers315" pmid="23264639" pmcid="PMC3528025" count="1">2013</citation>). <sentence_start/>In a model legume <italic toggle="yes">Medicago truncatula</italic>, six ZIP family transporters MtZIP1, MtZIP3, MtZIP4, MtZIP5, MtZIP6, and MtZIP7 have been tested for their ability to complement yeast heavy metals uptake mutants, and each family member was able to rescue the growth of Zn, Mn, and Fe uptake mutants, indicating their function in heavy metals transport (López-Millán et al., <citation rid="B251" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1023/B:PLAN.0000038271.96019.aa" pmid="15316291" count="1">2004</citation>).

Apart from the abovementioned transporters, recently another transporter arsenate reductase (ACR) has been characterized in yeast <italic toggle="yes">Saccharomyces cerevisiae</italic>, a model system for As resistance. <sentence_start/>It was reported that a 4.2-kb region conferred arsenite (AsIII) resistance in <italic toggle="yes">S. cerevisiae</italic>; they found three ACR genes, namely ACR1, ACR2, and ACR3 (Bobrowicz et al., <citation rid="B45" ref-type="bibr" pmid="9234670" doi="10.1002/(SICI)1097-0061(199707)13:9<819::AID-YEA142>3.0.CO;2-Y" count="1">1997</citation>). <sentence_start/>These authors also reported that ACR1 regulates ACR2 and ACR3 by transcriptional factor and any loss in ACR1 function yeast conferred arsenite and arsenate hypersensitivities (Bobrowicz et al., <citation rid="B45" ref-type="bibr" pmid="9234670" doi="10.1002/(SICI)1097-0061(199707)13:9<819::AID-YEA142>3.0.CO;2-Y" count="1">1997</citation>; Ghosh et al., <citation rid="B137" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.96.9.5001" pmid="10220408" pmcid="PMC21806" count="1">1999</citation>). <sentence_start/>Later on, Landrieu et al. (<citation rid="B224" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.0405248101" pmid="15329414" pmcid="PMC516575" count="1">2004a</citation>,<citation rid="B225" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.bbrc.2004.07.182" pmid="15336525" count="1">b</citation>) reported that ACR2 represents arsenate reductase that showed homology to yeast ASCR2 (ScACR2). <sentence_start/>Similarly, Ellis et al. (<citation rid="B102" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.106.084079" pmid="16766666" pmcid="PMC1533930" count="1">2006</citation>) reported other transporter PvACR2 from <italic toggle="yes">P. vittata</italic> and OsACR2.1 and OsACR2.3 from <italic toggle="yes">O. sativa</italic> (Duan et al., <citation rid="B97" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8137.2007.02009.x" pmid="17388894" count="1">2007</citation>). <sentence_start/>Earlier, ACR2 (called as CDC25) was thought to be involved in As metabolism in <italic toggle="yes">A. thaliana</italic>. <sentence_start/>Recent studies on <italic toggle="yes">A. thaliana</italic> have revealed the involvement of new arsenate reductase (ACR), namely HAC1 (Chao et al., <citation rid="B62" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pbio.1002009" pmid="25464340" pmcid="PMC4251824" count="1">2014</citation>) or ATQ1 (Sánchez-Bermejo et al., <citation rid="B343" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ncomms5617" pmid="25099865" count="1">2014</citation>). <sentence_start/>Chao et al. (<citation rid="B62" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pbio.1002009" pmid="25464340" pmcid="PMC4251824" count="1">2014</citation>) reported that loss of function of HAC1 in <italic toggle="yes">A. thaliana</italic> resulted in decreased As accumulation in roots, and thus, there was diminished As efflux to external medium. <sentence_start/>Another transporter, OsABCC1 localized in phloem cells of <italic toggle="yes">O. sativa</italic>, has been reported to be involved in sequestration of As to vacuole (Song et al., <citation rid="B389" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.1414968111" pmid="25331872" pmcid="PMC4226097" count="1">2014</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, in anaerobic paddy fields, As (mainly Arsenite) uptake is regulated by transporters of Si, namely Lsi1 (low silicon 1; influx transporter) and Lsi2 (low silicon 2; efflux transporters) (Ma et al., <citation rid="B255" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.0802361105" pmid="18626020" pmcid="PMC2481375" count="1">2008</citation>). <sentence_start/>Apart from these transporters, there are some other transporters as well that transfer arsenate and arsenite. <sentence_start/>Likewise, a transporter from <italic toggle="yes">P. vittata</italic>, PvACR3 has been reported to compartmentalize As into the vacuoles and loss in its function results in As hypersensitivity (Indriolo et al., <citation rid="B181" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1105/tpc.109.069773" pmid="20530755" pmcid="PMC2910956" count="1">2010</citation>).
Transcriptomics

Investigations on the basic mechanisms of heavy metal tolerance and adaptation are the area of great scientific interest and an intensive research. <sentence_start/>Various stressors induce an expression of a set of genes in plants (Nakashima et al., <citation rid="B297" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.108.129791" pmid="19126699" pmcid="PMC2613698" count="1">2009</citation>).

At molecular level, the regulation of gene expression is very important for the biological processes, which determines the fate of plant development as well as tolerance to heavy metal stress. <sentence_start/>Stressors trigger large number of genes and several proteins in order to link the signaling pathways that confer stress tolerance (Umezawa et al., <citation rid="B416" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.copbio.2006.02.002" pmid="16495045" count="1">2006</citation>; Valliyodan and Nguyen, <citation rid="B417" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.pbi.2006.01.019" pmid="16483835" count="1">2006</citation>; Manavalan et al., <citation rid="B258" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/pcp/pcp082" pmid="19546148" count="1">2009</citation>; Tran et al., <citation rid="B409" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4161/gmcr.1.1.10569" pmid="21912210" count="1">2010</citation>). <sentence_start/>These genes are classified into two groups: the regulatory genes and the functional genes (Tran et al., <citation rid="B409" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4161/gmcr.1.1.10569" pmid="21912210" count="1">2010</citation>). <sentence_start/>The genes of regulatory group encode various transcription factors (TFs), which can regulate various stress-responsive genes cooperatively and/or separately and thus, constitute a gene network. <sentence_start/>However, the genes of functional group encode metabolic compounds such as amines, alcohols, and sugars, which play a crucial role in heavy metal stress tolerance. <sentence_start/>The TFs, which are reported to be master regulators, control an expression of gene clusters and usually members of multigene families. <sentence_start/>Studies reveal that a single TF can control the expression of many target genes <italic toggle="yes">via</italic> specific binding of the TF to the cis-acting element in the promoters of its target genes (Wray et al., <citation rid="B446" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/molbev/msg140" pmid="12777501" count="1">2003</citation>; Nakashima et al., <citation rid="B297" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.108.129791" pmid="19126699" pmcid="PMC2613698" count="1">2009</citation>). <sentence_start/>Most of the TFs contain a DNA-binding domain that interacts with cis-regulatory elements in the promoters of its target genes and <italic toggle="yes">via</italic> a protein-protein interaction domain that helps in oligomerization of TFs with other regulators (Wray et al., <citation rid="B446" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/molbev/msg140" pmid="12777501" count="1">2003</citation>; Shiu et al., <citation rid="B373" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.105.065110" pmid="16166257" pmcid="PMC1203354" count="1">2005</citation>). <sentence_start/>This type of transcriptional regulatory system is referred as “regulon” (Nakashima et al., <citation rid="B297" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.108.129791" pmid="19126699" pmcid="PMC2613698" count="1">2009</citation>). <sentence_start/>Various TFs families such as AREB/ABF, MYB, AP2/EREBP, WRKY, bHLH, bZIP, MYC, HSF, DREB1/CBF, NAC, HB, ARID, EMF1, CCAAT-HAP2, CCAAT-DR1, CCAAT-HAP3, CCAAT-HAP5, C2H2, C3H, C2C2-Dof, C2C2-YABBY, C2C2-CO-like, C2C2-Gata, E2F-DP, ABI3VP1, ARF, AtSR, CPP, E2F-DP, SBP, MADS, TUB, etc. are known to influence stress response in plants (Singh et al., <citation rid="B378" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S1369-5266(02)00289-3" pmid="12183182" count="1">2002</citation>; Shiu et al., <citation rid="B373" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.105.065110" pmid="16166257" pmcid="PMC1203354" count="1">2005</citation>; Shameer et al., <citation rid="B358" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1155/2009/583429" pmid="19841686" pmcid="PMC2763139" count="1">2009</citation>). <sentence_start/>LeDuc et al. (<citation rid="B231" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.envpol.2006.01.008" pmid="16515825" count="1">2006</citation>), in a transcriptome analysis on plants, reported that plants treated with heavy metals could induce transcription factors that regulate corresponding transcriptional processes.

Liang et al. (<citation rid="B239" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10725-012-9743-x" count="1">2013</citation>) reported first FER regulatory gene involved in Fe uptake in tomato, and the functional analog of FER is FER-like Deficiency Induced Transcripition Factor (FIT) that has been conferred to play an important role under Fe deficiency in <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis</italic> (Yuan et al., <citation rid="B465" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/sj.cr.7290331" pmid="16117851" count="1">2005</citation>). <sentence_start/>In addition to this, there are several other subgroups of bHLH family <italic toggle="yes">viz</italic>., AtbHLH38, AtbHLH39, AtbHLH100, and AtbHLH101 that have been shown to be upregulated under Fe deficiency in roots and leaves of <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis</italic> (Wang et al., <citation rid="B431" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00425-007-0535-x" pmid="17516080" count="1">2007</citation>; Yuan et al., <citation rid="B466" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/cr.2008.26" pmid="18268542" count="1">2008</citation>). <sentence_start/>Later, several researchers proposed that AtbHLH38 or AtbHLH39 interacts with FIT and forms heterodimers and directly activates transcription factors for ferric chelate reductase and ferrous transporters, which are the two major genes regulating Fe uptake under deficient condition (Varotto et al., <citation rid="B420" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1046/j.1365-313X.2002.01381.x" pmid="12207649" count="1">2002</citation>; Vert et al., <citation rid="B425" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1105/tpc.001388" pmid="12084823" pmcid="PMC150776" count="1">2002</citation>; Yuan et al., <citation rid="B466" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/cr.2008.26" pmid="18268542" count="1">2008</citation>). <sentence_start/>In <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis</italic>, IRT1 has been reported to be the most essential ferrous transporter. <sentence_start/>Beside transporting Fe, it can also transport Zn, Mn, Co, Ni, and Cd, and thus, these metals get accumulated under Fe deficiency (Vert et al., <citation rid="B425" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1105/tpc.001388" pmid="12084823" pmcid="PMC150776" count="1">2002</citation>; Schaaf et al., <citation rid="B351" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1074/jbc.M601062200" pmid="16790430" count="1">2006</citation>). <sentence_start/>A recent study by Wu et al. (<citation rid="B448" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.111.190983" pmid="22184655" pmcid="PMC3271767" count="1">2012</citation>) in <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis</italic> revealed that expression of FIT with AtbHLH38 or AtbHLH39 further activates expression of several other transporters <italic toggle="yes">viz</italic>., HMA3, (MTP3), Iron Regulated Transporter2 (IRT2) that play regulatory role in maintaining Fe content under Cd exposure.

Transcriptome analysis in <italic toggle="yes">A. thaliana</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">B. juncea</italic> exposed to Cd stress has revealed the induction of basic region leucine zipper (bZIP) and zinc finger transcription factors (Ramos et al., <citation rid="B326" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.106.090894" pmcid="PMC1820930" pmid="17208961" count="1">2007</citation>). <sentence_start/>ERF1 and ERF5, two transcription factors belonging to AP2/ERF superfamily (characterized by AP2/ERF domain; Nakano et al., <citation rid="B295" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.105.073783" pmid="16407444" pmcid="PMC1361313" count="1">2006</citation>), have been reported to be induced when <italic toggle="yes">A. thaliana</italic> was exposed to Cd (Herbette et al., <citation rid="B164" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.biochi.2006.04.018" pmid="16797112" count="1">2006</citation>). <sentence_start/>Similar induction of TFs has been reported in <italic toggle="yes">A. halleri</italic> under Cd stress (Weber et al., <citation rid="B439" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1365-3040.2005.01479.x" pmid="17087478" count="1">2006</citation>). <sentence_start/>Differential expression of ERF factors under Cd indicates toward their responses to various levels of Cd stress. <sentence_start/>A study by Nakashima and Yamaguchi-Shinozaki (<citation rid="B296" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1399-3054.2005.00592.x" count="1">2006</citation>) reported down-regulation of dehydration-responsive element-binding protein (DREB) transcription factor (involved in cold and osmotic stress responsive genes) in roots of <italic toggle="yes">A. thaliana</italic> under heavy metal treatment and suggested it could be acclimation response and DREB might have helped in normalizing osmotic potential, so that flow of heavy metal-contaminated water could be reduced, thus helping plants to avoid toxic effects of heavy metal. <sentence_start/>Therefore, acquiring a deep knowledge of the interrelated mechanisms, which regulate the expression of these genes, is a crucial issue in plant biology and necessary to generate genetically improved crop plants for extreme environments like heavy metal stress (Umezawa et al., <citation rid="B416" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.copbio.2006.02.002" pmid="16495045" count="1">2006</citation>; Valliyodan and Nguyen, <citation rid="B417" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.pbi.2006.01.019" pmid="16483835" count="1">2006</citation>; Nakashima et al., <citation rid="B297" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.108.129791" pmid="19126699" pmcid="PMC2613698" count="1">2009</citation>). <sentence_start/>Summary of an involvement of TFs in conferring heavy metal and other abiotic stresses tolerance is given in Table 2.
Mitogen-activated protein kinase MAPK cascade

MAPK cascade are activated in response by plants when exposed to heavy metal stresses. <sentence_start/>This cascade has its significance in activation of signal transduction pathway used in hormone synthesis (Jonak et al., <citation rid="B192" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S1369-5266(02)00285-6" pmid="12183180" count="1">2002</citation>). <sentence_start/>This cascade involves three kinases <italic toggle="yes">viz</italic>., MAPK kinase kinase (MAPKKK), the MAPK kinase (MAPKK), and the MAPK, which are activated by phosphorylation process. <sentence_start/>The finally formed phosphorylated MAPK cascade phosphorylates substrates in cells including transcription factors in nucleus. <sentence_start/>Therefore, MAPK regulates the transduction of information downstream. <sentence_start/>Jonak et al. (<citation rid="B191" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.104.045724" pmid="15448198" pmcid="PMC523386" count="1">2004</citation>) have shown four isoforms of MAPK that are activated under Cu or Cd stress in <italic toggle="yes">Medicago sativa</italic>. <sentence_start/>All these pathways finally lead to regulation of transcription factors that in turn activate genes for activation of metal transporters, biosynthesis of chelating compounds, and other defensing compounds.
Proteomics

Proteomics is a well-established technique in the post-genomic era (Liu et al., <citation rid="B248" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0064041" pmid="23696864" pmcid="PMC3655940" count="1">2013</citation>). <sentence_start/>Proteomics deals with the study of large-scale expression of proteins in an organism encoded by its genome (Anderson and Anderson, <citation rid="B12" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/elps.1150191103" pmid="9740045" count="1">1998</citation>). <sentence_start/>Proteomics not only serves as a powerful tool for describing complete protein changes in any organisms but it can also be used to compare variation in protein profiles at organ, tissue, cell and organelle levels under various stress conditions including heavy metal stress (Ahsan et al., <citation rid="B7" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/pmic.200800935" pmid="19405030" count="1">2009</citation>). <sentence_start/>Although genomic analysis has enhanced our understanding regarding plants' response to heavy metal toxicity, transcriptomic changes in the genome are not always reflected at protein level (Gygi et al., <citation rid="B147" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1128/MCB.19.3.1720" pmid="10022859" pmcid="PMC83965" count="1">1999</citation>; Hossain and Komatsu, <citation rid="B175" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fpls.2012.00310" pmid="23355841" pmcid="PMC3555118" count="1">2013</citation>). <sentence_start/>For instance, putative Zn and Mg transporter protein MHX was more abundant in <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis</italic> even though its corresponding transcript level was not different (Elbaz et al., <citation rid="B100" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1365-3040.2006.01500.x" pmid="17080942" count="1">2006</citation>). <sentence_start/>This suggests that transcription of any gene is not a guaranty that gene would be translated into a functional protein. <sentence_start/>This may occur due to the potential impact of post-transcriptional and translational modifications, protein folding, stability and localization, protein-protein interactions, which are considered important determinants of a protein function (Dalcorso et al., <citation rid="B82" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fpls.2013.00280" pmid="23898342" pmcid="PMC3724048" count="1">2013b</citation>). <sentence_start/>Therefore, depth analyses of proteomics offer a new platform for identifying target proteins, which take part in heavy metal detoxification, and in studying complex biological processes and interactions among the possible pathways that involve a network of proteins (Ahsan et al., <citation rid="B7" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/pmic.200800935" pmid="19405030" count="1">2009</citation>).

Furthermore, it is known that proteins directly take part in plant stress responses, and plant adaptations to heavy metal stress are always accompanied with deep proteomic changes. <sentence_start/>Therefore, technique of proteomics can be exploited for deciphering the possible relationships between proteins abundance and plant stress adaptation. <sentence_start/>It can contribute to better understanding of physiological mechanisms under heavy metal stress such as perception of stress and further signaling cascade that leads to changes in the expression of huge numbers of genes at transcriptional level and in metabolite profile, which could be used for an acquisition of an enhanced plant tolerance under heavy metal toxicity (Kosová et al., <citation rid="B211" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jprot.2011.02.006" pmid="21329772" count="1">2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>Studies have revealed that an abundance of defense proteins was increased for scavenging of ROS, and molecular chaperones play a role in re-establishing the conformation of a functional protein that contributes in helping heavy metal stressed plants to maintain the redox homeostasis (Zhao et al., <citation rid="B477" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.chemosphere.2011.06.029" pmid="21723586" count="1">2011</citation>; Sharmin et al., <citation rid="B367" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.plantsci.2012.02.002" pmid="22404839" count="1">2012</citation>; Wang et al., <citation rid="B435" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/17429145.2011.603060" count="1">2012</citation>). <sentence_start/>Under heavy metal stress, modulations of various metabolic pathways occur such as photosynthesis, respiration, nitrogen metabolism, sulfur metabolism, etc. particularly in photosynthesis and mitochondrial respiration that help stressed plants to produce more reducing power such as NADPH, NADH, and FADH<sub>2</sub> and assimilatory power ATP to compensate high energy demand of heavy metal-challenged plants (Hossain and Komatsu, <citation rid="B175" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fpls.2012.00310" pmid="23355841" pmcid="PMC3555118" count="1">2013</citation>). <sentence_start/>For example, an increased abundance of RUBISCO large sub unit (LSU)-binding proteins, oxygen-evolving enhancer protein 1 and 2, NAD(P)H-dependent oxido-reductase, and photosystem I and II-related proteins is an adaptive feature to withstand heavy metal stress (Semane et al., <citation rid="B355" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jplph.2009.09.015" pmid="20005002" count="1">2010</citation>). <sentence_start/>The cellular mechanism of stress sensing and further transduction of signals into the cell appear to be the first reactions in the plant cell against heavy metal. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, an intracellular communication of stress signals plays a fundamental role in signal transduction pathways under stress, which ultimately activate defense-related genes and thus signaling cascades (Hossain et al., <citation rid="B176" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/pr200863r" pmid="22029473" count="1">2012c</citation>). <sentence_start/>Therefore, to decipher an underlying molecular mechanism of alterations in the protein signature of a plant cell in order to withstand stress, a deep study on the cellular as well as organelle proteomics would be of great importance in developing heavy metal-tolerant crops. <sentence_start/>Alterations in protein profile under heavy metal stress, which could be utilized for developing heavy metal-tolerant plants, are given in Table 3.

Apart from inducing synthesis of amino acids (proline and histidine), amines, organic acids, and plant antioxidant α-tocopherol and glutathione, some nitrogen containing metabolites like some peptides (phytochelatins, metallothioneins, and ferritins) have been reported to play an important role under heavy metal stress. <sentence_start/>In the following section, we will discuss about the roles of peptides in heavy metal tolerance.
Peptides

Phytochelatins (PCs) have been the best-characterized chelators in plant systems. <sentence_start/>PCs belong to a family of metal-binding protein having general structure (c-Glu-Cys)<italic toggle="yes">n</italic>Gly (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 2-11) (Cobbett and Goldsbrough, <citation rid="B75" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1146/annurev.arplant.53.100301.135154" pmid="12221971" count="1">2002</citation>). <sentence_start/>These are synthesized by the transpeptidation of the γ-Glu-Cys moiety of GSH, and the transpeptidation reactions are carried out by enzyme named phytochelatin synthase (PCS). <sentence_start/>It has been reported that PCS were activated under heavy metal exposure (Rauser, <citation rid="B328" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.109.4.1141" pmid="8539285" pmcid="PMC157644" count="1">1995</citation>; Cobbett, <citation rid="B74" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S1369-5266(00)00066-2" pmid="10837262" count="1">2000</citation>), and similar PC synthase activity has been observed in several other crops (Klapheck et al., <citation rid="B208" ref-type="bibr" pmid="12228379" doi="10.1104/pp.107.2.515" pmcid="PMC157155" count="1">1995</citation>; Chen et al., <citation rid="B65" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1399-3054.1997.tb01833.x" count="1">1997</citation>; Mishra et al., <citation rid="B278" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.biortech.2008.10.041" pmid="19091554" count="1">2009a</citation>). <sentence_start/>Loeffler et al. (<citation rid="B249" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/0014-5793(89)81611-4" count="1">1989</citation>) confirmed that metals induce PC synthesis, in <italic toggle="yes">in-vivo</italic> as well as in <italic toggle="yes">in-vitro</italic> cultures, and were continuously synthesized until activated metal ions chelated. <sentence_start/>Haag-Kerwer et al. (<citation rid="B148" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jxb/50.341.1827" count="1">1999</citation>) reported induction of PCs in <italic toggle="yes">B. juncea</italic> after the accumulation of Cd in the cells, and thus plays important role in detoxifying heavy metals (Hirata et al., <citation rid="B168" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1263/jbb.100.593" pmid="16473766" count="1">2005</citation>). <sentence_start/>Due to the presence of thiol group, they have the capability of chelating metals and forming complexes (Cobbett, <citation rid="B74" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S1369-5266(00)00066-2" pmid="10837262" count="1">2000</citation>), which are then sequestrated in the vacuole. <sentence_start/>From the preceding discussion, it is clear that chelation by PCs is not a simple process but involves a complex molecular mechanism, where firstly, the PCS gets activated by metal ion and biosynthesis of PCs takes place; secondly, formation of complexes and sequestration in vacuole; thirdly, more complexation with the sulfides or organic acids in the vacuole, and finally detoxified. <sentence_start/>Besides detoxifying heavy metals, PCs also play a major role in metal ion homeostasis and thus regulating the metal ion availability in plant cells (Guo et al., <citation rid="B145" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.108.115782" pmid="18287486" pmcid="PMC2287344" count="1">2008b</citation>).

Like PCs, metallothioneins (MTs) are synthesized and activated under heavy metal toxicity. <sentence_start/>They belong to a family of low molecular weight protein having cysteine-rich metal binding peptide. <sentence_start/>Due to the presence of mercaptides, they have the ability of binding metal ions. <sentence_start/>Metal-binding activities of MTs have been expressed in <italic toggle="yes">Escherichia coli</italic> in presence of Cd, Zn, and Cu (Tommey et al., <citation rid="B408" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/0014-5793(91)80831-M" pmid="1959626" count="1">1991</citation>). <sentence_start/>In addition, Zhou and Goldsbrough (<citation rid="B482" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1105/tpc.6.6.875" pmid="8061521" pmcid="PMC160485" count="1">1994</citation>) reported restoration in Cu tolerance ability of MT-deficient yeast strains, when provided with the <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis</italic> MTs. <sentence_start/>Similar to this, Zhigang et al. (<citation rid="B481" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jxb/erl102" pmid="16957018" count="1">2006</citation>) conferred increased tolerance of <italic toggle="yes">A. thaliana</italic> to Cd and Cu, when ectopically substituted with <italic toggle="yes">B. juncea</italic> MT. <sentence_start/>Moreover, comparative study of mutant and wild-type <italic toggle="yes">A. thaliana</italic> has clearly revealed that MT mutant was hypersensitive to Cd and accumulated much lower amount of Cd than wild type, thus conferring role of MTs in both heavy metal tolerance as well as accumulation (Zimeri et al., <citation rid="B486" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11103-005-8268-3" pmid="16240177" count="1">2005</citation>). <sentence_start/>In terms of transcript amount, expression of MT genes varies during different developmental stages of plant as well as under varying environmental condition (Rauser, <citation rid="B329" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/BF02738153" pmid="10505666" count="1">1999</citation>). <sentence_start/>Beside, chelating metal ions MTs can also catalyze antioxidant protection mechanism as well as plasma membrane repair (Hamer, <citation rid="B153" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1146/annurev.bi.55.070186.004405" pmid="3527054" count="1">1986</citation>).

Ferritins are other multimeric proteins that could accumulate iron atom (Harrison and Arosio, <citation rid="B156" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/0005-2728(96)00022-9" pmid="8695634" count="1">1996</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, animal ferritins have been reported to store other metals like Cu, Zn, Cd, etc., whereas plants ferritin could store only Fe. <sentence_start/>These are synthesized in plants when there is excess Fe in the surroundings and thus represents first-line defense against Fe-induced oxidative stress (Ravet et al., <citation rid="B330" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1365-313X.2008.03698.x" pmid="18826427" count="1">2009</citation>). <sentence_start/>These are not only involved in storing or releasing Fe but also involved in scavenging free reactive iron (Ravet et al., <citation rid="B330" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1365-313X.2008.03698.x" pmid="18826427" count="1">2009</citation>).
Plant growth hormones

In spite of five classical plant hormones, i.e., gibberellins (GAs), cytokinins (CKs), auxins, abscisic acid (ABA), and ethylene, jasmonate (JA), brassinosteroids (BR), and salicylic acid (SA) are also well known for regulating many physiological processes and heavy metal stress tolerance (Freeman et al., <citation rid="B124" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1128/AEM.71.12.8627-8633.2005" pmid="16332856" pmcid="PMC1317400" count="1">2005b</citation>; Gangwar et al., <citation rid="B133" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.scienta.2010.08.013" count="1">2010</citation>; Gangwar and Singh, <citation rid="B132" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.scienta.2011.03.026" count="1">2011</citation>; Peleg and Blumwald, <citation rid="B311" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.pbi.2011.02.001" pmid="21377404" count="1">2011</citation>; Choudhary et al., <citation rid="B73" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jxb/ers219" pmid="22915739" pmcid="PMC3444278" count="1">2012a</citation>,<citation rid="B72" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0033210" pmid="22479371" pmcid="PMC3315560" count="1">b</citation>; Vriet et al., <citation rid="B429" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1105/tpc.111.094912" pmid="22438020" pmcid="PMC3336137" count="1">2012</citation>). <sentence_start/>Furthermore, it is also expected that some more growth hormones are yet to be discovered in future. <sentence_start/>In laboratory as well as filed studies, two strategies have been used for plant hormone-mediated increase in stress tolerance as well as crop yield. <sentence_start/>These strategies include exogenous application of plant hormones and genetic manipulation of their endogenous contents. <sentence_start/>Both approaches have given promising results for increasing crop yield and enhancing stress tolerance in a variety of crop species (Vriet et al., <citation rid="B429" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1105/tpc.111.094912" pmid="22438020" pmcid="PMC3336137" count="1">2012</citation>). <sentence_start/>Although SA and GAs both are cost effective and can easily be availed for their exogenous application in crop fields under stress conditions, high cost of synthetic BRs and the variability of the results have discouraged the use of exogenous BRs in agriculture and horticulture (Khripach et al., <citation rid="B204" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1006/anbo.2000.1227" count="1">2000</citation>; Gomes, <citation rid="B140" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/978-94-007-0189-2_7" count="1">2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>In this context, modulation of endogenous BRs levels by genetic engineering has emerged an efficient strategy for enhancing crop yield under normal as well as adverse growth conditions (Divi and Krishna, <citation rid="B90" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nbt.2009.07.006" pmid="19631770" count="1">2009</citation>). <sentence_start/>Herein, we have summarized recent advances made in enhancing heavy metal tolerance as well as achieving high yield with desired agronomic traits by using salicylic acid (SA), brassinosteroids (BRs), and gibberellins (GA).
Salicylic acid (SA)

In recent years, SA has gained much scientific attention due to its function as an endogenous signaling molecule conveying local and systemic plant-pathogen defense responses. <sentence_start/>Besides this, it has been reported that SA also plays a role in plant response against abiotic stresses such as heavy metal toxicities, chilling, drought, osmotic stress, and heat. <sentence_start/>In this sense, SA appears to be an “effective therapeutic agent” for plants as in the case of mammals (Rivas-San Vicente and Plasencia, <citation rid="B334" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jxb/err031" pmid="21357767" count="1">2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>Salicylic acid is a phenolic compound biosynthesized in all the plant kingdoms through the phenylpropanoid pathway (Métraux, <citation rid="B270" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S1360-1385(02)02313-0" pmid="12167322" count="1">2002</citation>).

Being well characterized and studied role of SA in pathogen resistance, an exogenous application of SA could also provide protection against several types of abiotic stresses such as heavy metals, high or low temperature, salinity, radiation, etc. <sentence_start/>(Horváth et al., <citation rid="B171" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00344-007-9017-4" count="1">2007</citation>; Hayat et al., <citation rid="B159" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.envexpbot.2009.08.005" count="1">2010</citation>). <sentence_start/>Since under stress condition, reduced plant growth could result from an altered hormonal status, and thus, an exogenous application of plant hormones like SA has been an attractive approach to attenuate heavy metal stress. <sentence_start/>Studies carried out so far demonstrated that SA treatment to plants evoke acclimatization effect, which causes an enhanced tolerance toward heavy metal stress primarily due to the adjustment of metabolic processes such as enhanced antioxidative capacity. <sentence_start/>In one of the first works, it was demonstrated that SA may induce protective effects against Cu toxicity in tobacco and cucumber (Strobel and Kuc, <citation rid="B395" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1094/Phyto-85-1306" count="1">1995</citation>). <sentence_start/>Later, an increasing numbers of studies have demonstrated SA-mediated amelioration of toxicities produced by various heavy metals. <sentence_start/>Zhou et al. (<citation rid="B483" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.envexpbot.2008.06.001" count="1">2009</citation>) reported that 0.2 mM of SA ameliorates Hg toxicity in alfalfa by increasing activity of APX, POD, and NADPH oxidase, and amounts of ascorbate, glutathione, and proline, and decreased lipid peroxidation, and an increase in NADPH oxidase activity. <sentence_start/>It indicates a role of ROS signaling in such an amelioration process.

In maize plant, Cd declined the growth by inhibiting chlorophyll synthesis, ribulose 1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase and phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase, and enhancing oxidative damage such as lipid peroxidation and electrolyte leakage, whereas SA pretreatment of seeds reversed these toxic effects (Krantev et al., <citation rid="B218" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jplph.2006.11.014" pmid="17913285" count="1">2008</citation>). <sentence_start/>In cucumber, an exogenous application of SA has also been reported to enhance Mn tolerance by modulating nutrients' statuses and antioxidant defense system (Shi and Zhu, <citation rid="B369" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.envexpbot.2007.11.003" count="1">2008</citation>). <sentence_start/>Similarly, in pea seedlings, Cd toxicity caused decline in growth due to an inhabited photosynthetic process and enhanced oxidative damage, whereas SA pretreatment alleviated damaging consequences of Cd on growth and photosynthesis (Popova et al., <citation rid="B320" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.plaphy.2008.11.007" pmid="19091585" count="1">2009</citation>). <sentence_start/>Moreover, Guo et al. (<citation rid="B143" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jplph.2008.01.002" pmid="18313167" count="1">2009</citation>) have demonstrated that SA pretreatment alleviated Cd toxicity in rice by enhancing antioxidant components such as SOD, CAT, POD, glutathione, and non-protein thiols, which in turn depressed oxidative damage induced by Cd. <sentence_start/>Conversely, Metwally et al. (<citation rid="B271" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.102.018457" pmid="12746532" pmcid="PMC166972" count="1">2003</citation>) reported that SA down-regulates activities of antioxidant enzymes such as CAT and APX under Cd stress and concluded that SA alleviates Cd toxicity not at the level of antioxidant defense system but by affecting other mechanisms of Cd detoxification. <sentence_start/>Contrary to this, SA at higher concentration may also cause tissue damage and cell death by inducing oxidative stress (Horváth et al., <citation rid="B171" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00344-007-9017-4" count="1">2007</citation>). <sentence_start/>For instance, SA has been shown to potentiate generation of ROS in photosynthetic tissue under abiotic stresses and thus causes tissue damage (Borsani et al., <citation rid="B47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.126.3.1024" pmid="11457953" pmcid="PMC116459" count="1">2001</citation>). <sentence_start/>Therefore, it can be concluded that the concentration of SA appears to be important in regulating stress responses. <sentence_start/>The SA-mediated alterations in genes that are involved in mediating stress tolerance are listed in Table 4.

It is known that SA also involves in the regulation of oxidative stress caused by various stress factors (Yang et al., <citation rid="B460" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1365-313X.2004.02267.x" pmid="15584956" count="1">2004</citation>). <sentence_start/>An enhanced level of SA under heavy metal stress suggests a connection between the extent of plant tolerance to heavy metal, which is mediated by the SA signal and the redox balance (Metwally et al., <citation rid="B271" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.102.018457" pmid="12746532" pmcid="PMC166972" count="1">2003</citation>; Sharma and Dietz, <citation rid="B365" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.tplants.2008.10.007" pmid="19070530" count="1">2009</citation>). <sentence_start/>In the SA signaling under heavy metal stress, several signaling molecules such as nitric oxide (NO), H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, Ca<sup>+2</sup>, etc. and their interactions have been reported (Rodríguez-Serrano et al., <citation rid="B335" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1104/pp.108.131524" pmid="19279198" pmcid="PMC2675729" count="1">2009</citation>; Xu et al., <citation rid="B454" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10535-014-0475-9" count="1">2014</citation>). <sentence_start/>Moreover, Cui et al. (<citation rid="B80" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jxb/ers201" pmid="22915740" pmcid="PMC3444266" count="1">2012b</citation>) have reported a cross-talk of haem oxygenase-1 and SA in alleviation of Cd stress in <italic toggle="yes">M. sativa</italic>. <sentence_start/>In spite of considerable progress in the understanding of SA signaling, molecular events, which are involved in the SA signaling in order to alleviate heavy metal stress, are still poorly known (Figure 4).
