<bold>Schematic representation of plant hormone-mediated alleviation of heavy metal toxicity in plants</bold>. <sentence_start/>Heavy metals' signals are perceived by receptors, and receptors transduce signals <italic toggle="yes">via</italic> cAMP, pH, etc. causing alterations in electron transport systems of the cell, which results into an excess production of reactive oxygen species (ROS). <sentence_start/>ROS cause damage to macromolecules and thus create oxidative stress inside the cell. <sentence_start/>On the other hand, in the presence of plant hormones, signals received by them initiate a cascade of signal transduction involving haem oxygenase, two transcription factors induced by brassinosteroids (BES1 and BZR1) and a gibberellic acid-mediated GA-GID1-DELLA signaling pathway. <sentence_start/>These factors, in turn, initiate expression of the nuclear genes encoding defense proteins, transcription factors (TFs), heat shock proteins (HSP), and metal transporter proteins (MTs). <sentence_start/>MTs protect electron transport chains against heavy metals by regulating their uptake. <sentence_start/>Defense proteins protect plant against ROS under heavy metal stress (Numbers 1 and 2 designated to chloroplast and mitochondria show the sources of ROS in cell).
Brassinosteroids (BRs)

Brassinosteroids are group of hormones having ability of regulating ion uptake in plant cells and very effectively reducing the heavy metal accumulation in plants. <sentence_start/>BRs can also impart plant stress tolerance against variety of biotic and abiotic stresses such as heavy metal, salinity, drought, low and high temperatures, and pathogen attack (Bajguz and Hayat, <citation rid="B31" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.plaphy.2008.10.002" pmid="19010688" count="1">2009</citation>; Hao et al., <citation rid="B155" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00299-013-1438-x" pmid="23568410" count="1">2013</citation>). <sentence_start/>An increasing numbers of studies have shown that an exogenous application of BRs is widely used in order to improve crop yield as well as stress tolerance in various plant species (Divi and Krishna, <citation rid="B90" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nbt.2009.07.006" pmid="19631770" count="1">2009</citation>; Peleg and Blumwald, <citation rid="B311" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.pbi.2011.02.001" pmid="21377404" count="1">2011</citation>; Li et al., <citation rid="B236" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0066582" pmid="23840504" pmcid="PMC3686678" count="1">2013</citation>). <sentence_start/>Cadmium, a heavy metal, very toxic even when present in trace amount, have been found to retard chlorophyll biosynthesis, activity of several enzymes, and inhibit light and dark reactions of photosynthesis by limiting the energy/reducing sources (Vassilev and Yordanov, <citation rid="B421" ref-type="bibr" count="1">1997</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, it has been reported that Cd-induced toxicity can be lowered with BR. <sentence_start/>For instance, Janeckzo et al. (<citation rid="B187" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11099-005-0048-4" count="1">2005</citation>) reported that Cd-induced inhibition in pigments content, cotyledon growth could be minimized with exogenous epibrassinolide (EPL: another BR). <sentence_start/>Hayat et al. (<citation rid="B160" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.envexpbot.2006.06.002" count="1">2007</citation>) have verified the role of HBL under Cd stress in <italic toggle="yes">B. juncea</italic>. <sentence_start/>In <italic toggle="yes">Vigna radiata</italic> L. Wilczek, Al stress caused a reduction in length, fresh and dry mass of root and shoot; activity of carbonic anhydrase; water use efficiency; relative water content; chlorophyll content; and the rate of photosynthesis, whereas addition of BR reversed these toxic effects and protected the plants <italic toggle="yes">via</italic> elevated level of proline in an association with an antioxidant defense system which at least in part was responsible for the amelioration of Al stress (Ali et al., <citation rid="B9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.envexpbot.2007.07.014" count="1">2008</citation>). <sentence_start/>In <italic toggle="yes">B. juncea</italic>, BR alleviates Cd toxicity through enhanced level of antioxidants (Hayat et al., <citation rid="B160" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.envexpbot.2006.06.002" count="1">2007</citation>). <sentence_start/>The Cr, a known toxic metal, reduced the growth performance of <italic toggle="yes">Raphanus sativus</italic> L., whereas BR protects plants from adverse consequences of Cr toxicity by regulating antioxidant defense system (Sharma et al., <citation rid="B362" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10646-011-0650-0" pmid="21448625" count="1">2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>Micronutrients such as Cu and Ni are essential for growth and development, but in excess, they cause severe toxic effects. <sentence_start/>Cu, which has increasingly attained interest due to its use in fungicides, fertilizers, and pesticides, is also highly toxic to plants, but when seeds of <italic toggle="yes">B. juncea</italic> primed with epibrassinolide (a form of BR) were exposed to Cu stress, improvement in shoot emergence and biomass accumulation, along with reduced Cu uptake and accumulation, was noticed (Sharma and Bhardwaj, <citation rid="B363" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11738-007-0032-7" count="1">2007</citation>). <sentence_start/>Similar protective responses of exogenous BR on <italic toggle="yes">B. juncea</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">V. radiata</italic> under Cu and Ni toxicities have been reported (Alam et al., <citation rid="B8" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11099-007-0022-4" count="1">2007</citation>; Sharma et al., <citation rid="B364" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10535-008-0149-6" count="1">2008</citation>; Fariduddin et al., <citation rid="B110" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.envexpbot.2009.05.001" count="1">2009</citation>; Yusuf et al., <citation rid="B469" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11356-011-0531-3" pmid="21637971" count="1">2012b</citation>). <sentence_start/>Besides higher plants, BR has also been found to be effective in alleviating heavy metals such as Cu, Pb, and Cd toxicities in algae, <italic toggle="yes">Chlorella vulgaris</italic>, through the regulation of antioxidant defense system (Bajguz, <citation rid="B30" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.envexpbot.2009.11.003" count="1">2010</citation>). <sentence_start/>The BR-mediated alterations in the gene expressions and their roles in stress tolerance are listed in Table 2.
Gibberellic acid (GA)

The gibberellins (GAs) are a large family of tetracyclic diterpenoid plant growth hormone associated with the plant growth and developmental processes (Matsuoka, <citation rid="B263" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00344-003-0039-2" count="1">2003</citation>). <sentence_start/>To alleviate deleterious effects of stress, different types of plant hormones have been used that might complement decreased and/or imbalanced hormone level during exposure of stress. <sentence_start/>Of these, GA has been a focus of plant scientists (Hisamatsu et al., <citation rid="B170" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1034/j.1399-3054.2000.100114.x" count="1">2000</citation>; Iqbal et al., <citation rid="B183" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2011</citation>; Zhu et al., <citation rid="B485" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jhazmat.2012.08.077" pmid="23021314" count="1">2012</citation>).

Several studies revealed that GA alleviates various abiotic stresses including heavy metal toxicity. <sentence_start/>In <italic toggle="yes">A. thaliana</italic>, GA (5 μM) is reported to ameliorate Cd toxicity by reducing Cd uptake and lipid peroxidation (Zhu et al., <citation rid="B485" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jhazmat.2012.08.077" pmid="23021314" count="1">2012</citation>). <sentence_start/>Furthermore, authors demonstrated that GA reduces NO level which in turn down-regulates expression of <italic toggle="yes">IRT1</italic> gene, a Fe transporter (might be involved in Cd absorption) as indicated by no effect of GA in reduction of Cd uptake in an IRT1 knockout mutant <italic toggle="yes">irt1</italic>. <sentence_start/>It is reported that an exogenous addition of GA reprograms the growth of soybean under stress conditions by enhancing the levels of daidzein and genistein contents, suggesting protective role of GA in mitigating adverse consequences of stressors (Hamayun et al., <citation rid="B152" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/jf101221t" pmid="20509656" count="1">2010</citation>). <sentence_start/>In wheat seedlings, Ni (50 mM) has been shown to decline growth, chlorophyll content, and carbonic anhydrase activity by enhancing oxidative stress, whereas an addition of GA ameliorates Ni-induced toxic effects (Siddiqui et al., <citation rid="B375" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00709-010-0197-6" pmid="20730631" count="1">2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>Gangwar et al. (<citation rid="B134" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11738-010-0672-x" count="1">2011</citation>) have also reported that an exogenous addition of GA ameliorates toxic effects of Cr (50-250 μM) on growth and ammonium assimilation of pea seedlings by regulating oxidative stress and an antioxidant system. <sentence_start/>In <italic toggle="yes">B. napus</italic> L., GA (50 μM) has been shown to alleviate Cd (10-400 μM)-induced negative impact on seed germination and growth by regulating oxidative stress and damage (Meng et al., <citation rid="B268" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10725-008-9351-y" count="1">2009</citation>). <sentence_start/>It has been observed that Pb and Zn affect seed germination in <italic toggle="yes">Cicer arietinum</italic> cv. <sentence_start/>Aziziye-94 by altering hormonal balance, and an exogenous application of GA reverses the toxic effect of heavy metals (Atici et al., <citation rid="B25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10535-005-5222-9" count="1">2005</citation>). <sentence_start/>Furthermore, Sharaf et al. (<citation rid="B361" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2009</citation>) have also reported that GA mitigates detrimental effects of Cd and Pb on broad bean and lupin plants by regulating activities of proteases, CAT, and POD. <sentence_start/>These studies clearly indicate that GA plays an important role in protecting plant metabolism against various stresses; however, this may occur <italic toggle="yes">via</italic> various routes suggesting complex GA signaling during plant acclimation against stresses. <sentence_start/>The GA-mediated alterations in genes and their relation with stress tolerance are summarized in Table 4.
Conclusion and future prospects

Around 3.1 billion people from developing countries live in rural areas, and out of this population, ~2.5 billion people depend on agricultural practices for their livelihood, which contributes 30% to economic growth because of the gross domestic products obtained from agriculture (FAO, <citation rid="B108" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2012</citation>). <sentence_start/>It is expected that world population will be about 10 billion by the middle of the twenty-first century, and we will witness serious food shortages (Smith et al., <citation rid="B386" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1098/rstb.2010.0127" pmid="20713395" pmcid="PMC2935113" count="1">2010</citation>; Naika et al., <citation rid="B294" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/pcp/pcs185" pmid="23314754" pmcid="PMC3583027" count="1">2013</citation>). <sentence_start/>Furthermore, the situation will likely to be severe due to increased anthropogenic activities that have resulted into unwanted changes in the environment such as soil, air, and water pollution with various factors including heavy metal. <sentence_start/>These situations (pollution and population) are posing a continuously increasing burden on global crop productivity, and hence, there are demands for crop varieties that should be adaptive and resistant to various stresses.

In contrast to biotic stress, which is under the control of monogenic trait, abiotic stress tolerance is a genetically complex process that involves many components of signaling pathways, multigenic in nature, and thus, comparatively more difficult to control and engineer (Vinocur and Altman, <citation rid="B427" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.copbio.2005.02.001" pmid="15831376" count="1">2005</citation>). <sentence_start/>Therefore, plant-engineering strategies for heavy metal tolerance depend on the expression of gene(s) whose product(s) are involved either in signaling and regulatory pathways or in the synthesis of functional and structural proteins and metabolites that confer heavy metal stress tolerance. <sentence_start/>Recently, several efforts are being made to improve heavy metal stress tolerance capacity through genetic engineering with several achievements; however, the genetically complex mechanisms of heavy metal stress tolerance and transfer of technology to field conditions make it difficult. <sentence_start/>Advances in various functional tools, resources, and “omics” have helped in the molecular characterization of the genes, metabolites, and proteins involved in heavy metal stress tolerance. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, genetic engineering of heavy metal-responsive genes (particularly TFs), metabolites, and proteins has shown surprising results but its full potential remains to be exploited. <sentence_start/>The design of future experiments that use a multidisciplinary approach with well-integrated “omics,” i.e., transcritomics, metabolomics, proteomics, etc. ultimately required to significantly improve heavy metal tolerance as well as tolerance to other abiotic stresses in economically important crop plants.
